n:
- The phrase "There once was a man" can begin a parable (symbolic story with asocial meanings) or a historical account ({{2 Samuel 12:1|2 Samuel 12:1}}; {{1 Samuel 25:2|1 Samuel 25:2}}).

- {{Ezekiel 14:14|Ezekiel 14:14}}, {{Ezekiel 14:20|20}} and {{James 5:11|James 5:11}}also mention Job.

- *Uz* is east of the Jordan River, either in Edom to the south or in Aram to the north ({{Genesis 36:28|Genesis 36:28}}; {{1 Chronicles 1:42|1 Chronicles 1:42}}; {{Jeremiah 25:19-20|Jeremiah 25:19–20}}; {{Lamentations 4:21|Lamentations 4:21}}; {{Genesis 10:23|Genesis 10:23}}; {{Genesis 22:21|22:21}}; {{1 Chronicles 1:17|1 Chronicles 1:17}}, {{1 Chronicles 1:42|42}}). *Job* was not from Israel. He lived before the nation of Israel existed and outside its later territory.

- *Job* had no moral faults, he was a man of complete integrity ({{Job 1:8|Job 1:8}}; {{Job 2:3|2:3}}; see {{Psalm 25:21|Psalms 25:21}}; {{Psalm 37:37|37:37}}; {{Proverbs 2:7|Proverbs 2:7}}; {{Proverbs 20:11|20:11}}; {{Proverbs 29:10|29:10}}). He did not claim to be perfect or without sin ({{Job 6:24|Job 6:24}}; {{Job 7:21|7:21}}; see also {{Ecclesiastes 7:20|Ecclesiastes 7:20}}; {{Romans 3:23|Romans 3:23}}; {{1 John 1:8|1 John 1:8}}). But he was righteous (in a right relationship with God) so his suffering was not because of guilt. Here, *fearing God* probably means he did not worship any Ancient Near Eastern gods (see {{Psalm 111:10|Psalms 111:10}}; {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}; {{Proverbs 9:10|9:10}}; {{2 Corinthians 7:1|2 Corinthians 7:1}}; {{Job 9:8|Job 9:8}}; {{Job 23:13|23:13}}; {{Job 31:26-28|31:26–28}}).

Job had everything that people in his time could hope for. He had a large family and many servants. He was a successful farmer of livestock. He was highly respected and had authority in the area where he lived.

He was also completely committed to God. He did what God wanted done. He showed how much he respected God by making sacrifices. He did this when his family sinned. He even did it when he thought they might have sinned.

He wanted everyone in his family to live in ways that were considered pure and clean. This would allow them to worship God together.
God and Satan agree to test Job, which causes his troubles and confirms his integrity ({{Job 1:20-21|1:20–21}}; {{Job 2:10|2:10}}). None of the book's characters ever learn of this council in heaven.

- God gave* Job* prosperity with many *sons, daughters*, cattle and other domestic animals, and *servants* (compare {{Genesis 30:43|Genesis 30:43}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:13|Deuteronomy 7:13}}; {{Psalm 107:38|Psalm 107:38}}).

- Numbers like *seven* and *three* (and *7,000* and *3,000*) show the full extent of God's blessings for Job (see {{Job 42:13|Job 42:13}}; also see {{Psalm 127:3-5|Psalms 127:3–5}}; {{Psalm 128:3|128:3}}).

- *Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East*: The numbers describing Job’s wealth might not be exact, but they are realistic for a wealthy man of that time (compare Nabal’s wealth in {{1 Samuel 25:2|1 Samuel 25:2}}).

- People often washed and changed clothes to *purify* themselves before making a sacrifice ({{Genesis 35:2|Genesis 35:2}}; {{Exodus 19:10|Exodus 19:10}}, {{Exodus 19:14|14}}).

- The usual time for sincere religious dedication was early morning (see {{Genesis 22:3|Genesis 22:3}}; {{Psalm 5:3|Psalm 5:3}}; {{Mark 1:35|Mark 1:35}}). 

- *cursed*: The Hebrew verb *barak* (usually meaning *blessed*) used here is a polite way to say "cursed" (compare {{Job 1:11|Job 1:11}}; {{Job 2:5|2:5}}, {{Job 2:9|9}}; {{1 Kings 21:10|1 Kings 21:10}}, {{1 Kings 21:13|13}}; {{Psalm 10:3|Psalm 10:3}}). Job worried that his children might have committed this serious crime ({{Leviticus 24:10-16|Leviticus 24:10–16}}; {{1 Kings 21:9-13|1 Kings 21:9–13}}; compare {{Job 1:11|Job 1:11}}; {{Job 2:5|2:5}}, {{Job 2:9|9}}). Job knew that God regards wrong attitudes as sin ({{Jeremiah 17:9-10|Jeremiah 17:9–10}}; {{Mark 7:21-23|Mark 7:21–23}}).

- These *sons of God *are spiritual beings and members of the court of heaven. They are probably either holy angels or demons ({{Genesis 6:2|Genesis 6:2}}, {{Genesis 6:4|4}}). They join God in his discussions, including during creation and in his rule over creation ({{Genesis 1:26|Genesis 1:26}}; {{Job 1:6|Job 1:6}}; {{Genesis 3:22|Genesis 3:22}}; {{Genesis 2:1|2:1}}; {{1 Kings 22:19-22|1 Kings 22:19–22}}; {{Psalm 82:1|Psalms 82:1}}; {{Psalm 89:5|89:5}}, {{Psalm 89:7-8|7–8}}; {{Daniel 3:13|Daniel 3:13}}, {{Daniel 3:17|17}}, {{Daniel 3:23|23}}, {{Daniel 3:25|25}}; {{Daniel 7:9-14|7:9–14}}).

- It is uncertain in the account if *Satan* usually came with other court members of heaven to report or if he forced his way in as Job’s opponent.

- *"Where have you come from?"*: This question was God’s command for a report from one of his subjects (see {{Genesis 3:9|Genesis 3:9}}).

- *Satan* was not *roaming through the earth* to do God’s will (compare {{1 Chronicles 21:1-14|1 Chronicles 21:1–14}}; {{2 Kings 19:35|2 Kings 19:35}} is equivalent to {{Isaiah 37:36|Isaiah 37:36}}; {{Ezekiel 1:5-9|Ezekiel 1:5–9}}). Instead, he opposes God’s plans ({{2 Timothy 2:26|2 Timothy 2:26}}; {{1 Peter 5:8|1 Peter 5:8}}).

God wanted Satan to notice Job. Later Satan was understood to be the devil. Satan brought a charge against Job. He accused Job of only serving God because of the ways that God blessed him.

Satan wanted God to test Job. He was sure that Job would speak evil things against God. He would do this if he were made to suffer. This meant that Job would stop honouring God.

God gave Satan the authority to take away everything Job had except his life. First Satan took away Job’s livestock, his servants and his children. Job remained humble before God as he mourned. He recognised that God had allowed him to have good things. And he recognised that God had allowed them to be taken away.

Job recognised that God had the right to decide what happened in his life. He praised the name of the Lord even in his sadness.

Then Satan took away Job’s health. Job’s body was in pain. He sat in ashes. This was a common practice to show that people were very sad. Job’s wife saw how miserable he was. She thought that it would be better for him to die. She suggested that Job speak against God so that God would put him to death. Job thought that this idea was foolish. The wise thing to do was to remain faithful to God no matter what happened.

*My servant*: 

People used this title for:

- The patriarchs ("first fathers") of Israel ({{Genesis 26:24|Genesis 26:24}}; {{Exodus 32:13|Exodus 32:13}}).

- The prophets ({{2 Kings 17:13|2 Kings 17:13}}; {{Jeremiah 7:25|Jeremiah 7:25}}; {{Zechariah 1:6|Zechariah 1:6}}).

- King David (for example, {{2 Samuel 7:1-29|2 Samuel 7:1–29}}; {{Psalm 18:1|Psalms 18:1}}; {{Psalm 36:1|36:1}}).

*Job* has a good reason (Hebrew *khinnam*; see study note on 2:3) to *fear God*. The wisdom tradition connects being religious with prosperity. Satan suggested that Job's dedication to God depended on his wealth.
*a hedge on every side*: See {{1 Samuel 25:16|1 Samuel 25:16}}; {{Psalm 5:12|Psalms 5:12}}; {{Psalm 34:7|34:7}}; {{Zechariah 2:5|Zechariah 2:5}}; compare {{Isaiah 5:5|Isaiah 5:5}}.

- *Stretch out … and strike all he has … Everything he has is in your hands:* Satan was God's agent. The *hand* he used was both the Lord's and Satan's. They acted against everything Job owned and later against Job himself ({{Job 2:5-6|2:5–6}}).

- Job later cursed the day of his birth, but he did not curse God ({{Job 3:1|3:1}}, {{Job 3:8|8}}; {{Job 31:30|31:30}}). This was even true when his upset wife urged him to do so ({{Job 2:9|2:9}}).

- God allowed Satan to test Job to show that Satan's negative view of Job was wrong ({{1 Corinthians 10:11|1 Corinthians 10:11}}; see {{James 1:13|James 1:13}}; compare {{Luke 22:31-32|Luke 22:31–32}}; {{John 19:11|John 19:11}}).

- These attacks took away the blessings listed in {{Job 1:2-3|1:2–3}}. Job was left with four messengers who came to report terrible news and a wife who gave poor advice.

- The phrase "*While he was still speaking*" emphasizes the repeated nature of the attacks (see {{Jeremiah 51:31|Jeremiah 51:31}}). The phrase "*I alone have escaped to tell you*" emphasizes the complete destruction of Job’s resources.

*The Sabeans* were tribes who raided from the desert (compare {{Judges 6:3|Judges 6:3}}). By the 700s BC, the southern *Sabeans* became a powerful nation. They traded in gold, precious stones, sweet smelling liquids, and slaves (see {{Psalm 72:10|Psalm 72:10}}; {{Isaiah 43:3|Isaiah 43:3}}; {{Isaiah 45:14|45:14}}; {{Isaiah 60:6|60:6}}; {{Jeremiah 6:20|Jeremiah 6:20}}).

*The fire of God … from heaven*: This might have been lightning, fire in the desert, or the activity of a volcano ({{Job 20:26|20:26}}; {{Leviticus 10:2|Leviticus 10:2}}; {{1 Kings 18:38|1 Kings 18:38}}; {{2 Kings 1:10-14|2 Kings 1:10–14}}; {{Numbers 11:1-3|Numbers 11:1–3}}; {{Genesis 19:24|Genesis 19:24}}).
*a mighty wind …struck the four corners of the house*: This suggests that Job and his children were farmers settled and living in houses, not people wandering about and living in tents (nomads).

- *Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head*: These were common ceremonies in the Ancient Near East to show grief. People sometimes responded this way instead of harming themselves when shocked, in horror, or after hearing bad news ({{Job 2:12|2:12}}; {{Genesis 37:29|Genesis 37:29}}, {{Genesis 37:34|34}}; {{Judges 11:35|Judges 11:35}}; {{Jeremiah 16:6|Jeremiah 16:6}}; {{Ezekiel 7:18|Ezekiel 7:18}}; {{Amos 8:10|Amos 8:10}}).

- *He fell to the ground and worshiped*: Then in an unexpected move, *Job* did not give a desperate cry, but had hope ({{1 Peter 5:6|1 Peter 5:6}}).
This scene repeats exactly as it did in {{Job 1:6-8|1:6–8}}.
The phrase *without cause* (Hebrew *khinnam*) is a play on words from Satan's question in {{Job 1:9|1:9}}.
*strike his flesh and bones*: People once believed *bones* were the source of health.
*spare* (literally *guard *or* watch over*): Ironically, God made Satan responsible for guarding Job’s life (compare {{Job 10:13-14|10:13–14}}; {{Job 13:27|13:27}}; {{Job 33:11|33:11}}).

This Hebrew term for *terrible boils* referred to any raised wounds that leak ({{Exodus 9:10|Exodus 9:10}}; {{Leviticus 13:18-20|Leviticus 13:18–20}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:27|Deuteronomy 28:27}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:35|35}}).

- *Job* might have scraped his skin for relief. The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) says it was “to scrape away the pus.” 

- *The ashes* might refer to a place where they placed lepers in isolation. But Job was probably showing his grief and how desperate he was ({{Job 30:19|30:19}}; {{Genesis 18:27|Genesis 18:27}}; {{2 Samuel 13:19|2 Samuel 13:19}}; {{Isaiah 58:5|Isaiah 58:5}}; {{Jonah 3:6|Jonah 3:6}}).

*Job's wife* first summarized Job's temptation by echoing God's words. Job was trying to "retain his *integrity*" ({{Job 2:3|2:3}}). In her frustration and pain, she then advised Job to* curse God*. Without knowing it, she was asking Job to fulfill Satan's prediction ({{Job 1:11|1:11}}; {{Job 2:5|2:5}}).

- *Job* accepted both good and bad things *from God*, showing his right relationship and faith in God (righteousness) (compare {{Job 1:21|1:21}}; {{2 Samuel 12:16-20|2 Samuel 12:16–20}}; {{Luke 22:42|Luke 22:42}}).

- By saying nothing wrong, *Job* controlled his tongue ({{Proverbs 13:3|Proverbs 13:3}}; {{Proverbs 21:23|21:23}}; see {{James 3:2|James 3:2}}).

- It might have taken several months for *Job’s three friends* to learn about his troubles (see study note on 6:14–27; see {{Job 7:3|7:3}}). 

- The text suggests that *Job’s three friends* were Edomites, a people known for their wisdom ({{Jeremiah 49:7|Jeremiah 49:7}}; {{Obadiah 8|Obadiah 1:8}}). 

- *Eliphaz the Temanite *was probably a descendant of Esau’s grandson Teman ({{Genesis 36:10-11|Genesis 36:10–11}}, {{Genesis 36:15|15}}). His land was in Edom ({{Ezekiel 25:13|Ezekiel 25:13}}; {{Amos 1:11-12|Amos 1:11–12}}). 

- The "Bil-" part of the name "Bildad" would remind Hebrew readers of names like *Bilhan,* a descendant of Esau ({{Genesis 36:27|Genesis 36:27}}; {{1 Chronicles 1:42|1 Chronicles 1:42}}). The "*-*dad" part of the name would remind readers of names like *Bedad,* father of the Edomite king *Hadad* ({{Genesis 36:35|Genesis 36:35}}; {{1 Chronicles 1:46|1 Chronicles 1:46}}). 

- *Shuhite*: No place named "Shuah" is known, but Abraham’s son "Shuah" was sent to “a land in the east” ({{Genesis 25:1|Genesis 25:1}}, {{Genesis 25:6|6}}; {{1 Chronicles 1:32|1 Chronicles 1:32}}).

- The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) lists *Zophar* instead of "Zepho" as one of Esau’s grandsons ({{Genesis 36:11|Genesis 36:11}}, {{Genesis 36:15|15}}; {{1 Chronicles 1:36|1 Chronicles 1:36}}). A *Naamathite* might live in a town named "Naamah." But no such place is known. Two Old Testament women are named "Naamah," but neither is likely an ancestor of *Zophar* ({{Genesis 4:22|Genesis 4:22}}; {{1 Kings 14:21|1 Kings 14:21}}).

Job’s friends Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar visited him in order to comfort him. These men joined Job in his sadness. They recognised how terribly Job was suffering.

They did several things that were common in that time for people who were mourning. They also showed their respect for Job by being silent for seven days. They waited for Job to speak first.

His speech was recorded as a long poem. Job described how sad and bitter his life had become. He didn’t have any peace or rest. He wished that he hadn’t been born.

Job wondered why God allowed people who were suffering to continue living.

- *They could barely recognize Job*: This expression shows how much *Job* had suffered (compare {{Isaiah 52:14|Isaiah 52:14}}; {{Isaiah 53:3|53:3}}). 

- Job’s friends showed their grief and *began to weep aloud*, as if Job was dead. 

- Throwing *dust* sometimes showed anger or hate (see {{2 Samuel 16:13|2 Samuel 16:13}}; {{Acts 22:23|Acts 22:23}}). But here it showed grief (see {{Joshua 7:6|Joshua 7:6}}; {{1 Samuel 4:12|1 Samuel 4:12}}; {{Nehemiah 9:1|Nehemiah 9:1}}; {{Lamentations 2:10|Lamentations 2:10}}).

- Job’s friends *sat on the ground* to share in Job’s suffering (see {{Job 2:8|2:8}}).

- People usually showed grief for seven days and nights when an important person died or to acknowledge other bad news ({{Genesis 50:10|Genesis 50:10}}; {{1 Samuel 31:13|1 Samuel 31:13}}; see also {{Ezekiel 3:14-15|Ezekiel 3:14–15}}).

- Job spoke and risked words of sin ({{Job 1:21|1:21}}; {{Job 2:10|2:10}}).

- Job *cursed the day of his birth* in great detail. However, his words sounded more like sad complaints. Job did not curse God as his creator, but he showed grief about the condition of his life.

Job's outbreak of emotion did not mean his integrity failed under pressure ({{Job 42:7-8|42:7–8}}; {{James 5:11|James 5:11}}). The prophets Elijah and Jeremiah, both men of God, exaggerated with similar language ({{1 Kings 19:4|1 Kings 19:4}}; {{Jeremiah 20:14-18|Jeremiah 20:14–18}}).

Job wished that the *darkness* of the place of the dead and the *gloom* of death had not allowed him to be born ({{Exodus 10:22|Exodus 10:22}}; {{Proverbs 4:19|Proverbs 4:19}}; {{Joel 2:2|Joel 2:2}}; {{Job 10:21-22|Job 10:21–22}}; {{Job 38:17|38:17}}).
The phrase *those who curse the day* refers to people paid to *curse*, like Balaam ({{Numbers 22:1-24:25|Numbers 22–24}}).
Venus and Mercury, known as the *morning stars,* announce the arrival of *dawn* ({{Job 38:7|38:7}}).

*shut the doors of the womb*: Closing or opening *the womb* can mean conception ({{Genesis 16:2|Genesis 16:2}}; {{Genesis 20:18|20:18}}; {{Genesis 29:31|29:31}}; {{Genesis 30:22|30:22}}; {{1 Samuel 1:5-6|1 Samuel 1:5–6}}). But here it means birth (see also {{Job 38:8|Job 38:8}}).

Job's language shifts from wishing he was never born to grief. He goes from hating life towards an attraction for death. Job asks "why" seven times, as he has grief for his situation ({{Job 3:11|3:11}}, {{Job 3:12|12}}, {{Job 3:16|16}}, {{Job 3:20|20}}, {{Job 3:23|23}}; see {{Psalm 10:1|Psalms 10:1}}; {{Psalm 22:1|22:1}}; {{Jeremiah 20:18|Jeremiah 20:18}}; {{Lamentations 5:20|Lamentations 5:20}}).
People believed the dead kept their identities and social status. Job might have wanted kings and prime ministers to recognize his status as a prince ({{Job 1:3|1:3}}).

*who had gold, who filled their houses with silver*: This might refer to tombs filled with treasure. However, it more likely refers to the useless storing of wealth that ends in death (as in {{Job 3:14|3:14}}).

- Job compared *light* to *life* ({{Job 33:30|33:30}}; see {{John 1:4|John 1:4}}; {{John 8:12|8:12}}).

- *Bitter* might mean:

- “Angry” ({{Judges 18:25|Judges 18:25}}).

- “Fierce” ({{2 Samuel 17:8|2 Samuel 17:8}}).

- “Anguish” ({{Job 7:11|Job 7:11}}).

- Desperate ({{Proverbs 31:6|Proverbs 31:6}}).

- “Distress” ({{1 Samuel 1:10|1 Samuel 1:10}}; {{1 Samuel 22:2|22:2}}).
People in grief desperately *long for death*, like those who *search* for *hidden treasure.*

- *Eliphaz the Temanite* was probably the oldest and most important of Job’s friends (see study note on 2:11). His speeches are longer and more detailed than the others.

- *who can keep from speaking?: Eliphaz* imitated how urgent a message from prophets can be ({{Job 4:12-16|4:12–16}}; see {{Jeremiah 20:9|Jeremiah 20:9}}; {{Amos 3:8|Amos 3:8}}).

This section starts three rounds of speeches by Job's three "comforters," each followed by Job's response ({{Job 4:1-27:23|4:1–27:23}}). In the first round, Job's friends urge him to seek God to regain prosperity.

Eliphaz and Bildad each spoke three times. Zophar spoke twice. All of their speeches are recorded as long poems.

Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar explained the reason why they thought Job was suffering. Throughout his life, Eliphaz had noticed that trouble came to foolish people. Suffering was how they were taught as well as punished for their sins. Eliphaz believed that this was a pattern for how things work in the world. He believed that it was happening in Job’s case.

Bildad had noticed that God didn’t bring judgement against people who hadn’t sinned. This was a lesson that people had taught for hundreds of years. Bildad believed it was a pattern for how things work in the world. So he thought that Job and his family were being punished for their sins.

Zophar was sure that ungodly people are always punished. He believed that this is how things had always been in the world. He was sure that God was bringing judgement on Job for sins Job had committed.

Job answered Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar each time after they spoke. Job was sad and angry because his friends said things that weren’t helpful. Many of the things they said were true. But the patterns they noticed in life didn’t apply to Job’s case. Job hadn’t sinned in secret. Job didn’t claim to have never sinned. But he knew that God wasn’t punishing him for his sins. Job knew that he had lived the way God wanted people to live. His friends didn’t understand him. They accused him falsely.

Job believed that God did understand him. Job believed that God knew that he wasn’t guilty of secret sins. Job wanted God to explain why his life had become so difficult. Job was very confused by God and angry at him. But Job continued to have respect for God and to avoid evil. He did this even though he was suffering terribly. This showed that Job had wisdom and understanding.
These were people who were weak, felt depressed, and had low confidence in themselves ({{Isaiah 13:7|Isaiah 13:7}}; {{Isaiah 35:3|35:3}}; {{Ezekiel 7:17|Ezekiel 7:17}}).

Job probably considered his children among the *innocent* who died ({{Job 1:5|1:5}}). Even Eliphaz must have known that people sometimes "shed innocent blood" (compare {{Deuteronomy 19:10|Deuteronomy 19:10}}; {{Proverbs 6:17|Proverbs 6:17}}; {{Jeremiah 7:6|Jeremiah 7:6}}).

The symbolic use of the language of harvest shows the idea in the Scriptures that actions deserve judgment ({{Proverbs 22:8|Proverbs 22:8}}; {{Hosea 8:7|Hosea 8:7}}; {{Romans 2:9-11|Romans 2:9–11}}; {{Galatians 6:7-8|Galatians 6:7–8}}). The New Testament compares the final judgment to a harvest ({{Matthew 13:39|Matthew 13:39}}). By this principle, Jesus rejected overly simple attempts to analyze people's lives ({{Luke 13:4|Luke 13:4}}; {{John 9:1-3|John 9:1–3}}).
*by the blast of His anger they are consumed*: Eliphaz saw the wind in {{Job 1:19|1:19}} as God's judgment (compare {{Isaiah 40:7|Isaiah 40:7}}; {{Hosea 13:15|Hosea 13:15}}).
Eliphaz claimed to be a prophet, suggesting that God spoke to him *secretly* ({{Numbers 12:6|Numbers 12:6}}). Later, God did speak to him, but not to support his advice ({{Job 42:7|Job 42:7}}).

Eliphaz probably referred to the sleep caused by God that links to the *visions* given to prophets ({{Job 33:15|33:15}}; {{Genesis 15:12|Genesis 15:12}}; {{Numbers 12:6|Numbers 12:6}}; {{Isaiah 29:10|Isaiah 29:10}}).

- *Fear* often occurs in God's presence ({{Genesis 15:12|Genesis 15:12}}; {{Daniel 8:17-18|Daniel 8:17–18}}; {{Daniel 10:8-10|10:8–10}}). But God tells his people not to *fear* ({{Genesis 15:1|Genesis 15:1}}; {{Genesis 26:24|26:24}}; {{Isaiah 40:9|Isaiah 40:9}}; {{Isaiah 44:8|44:8}}).

- Eliphaz's *bones* shook like those of a prophet with terrible news to share ({{Jeremiah 23:9|Jeremiah 23:9}}; {{Habakkuk 3:16|Habakkuk 3:16}}).

*a spirit *(or* wind*)* glided past my face*: Wind shows God's powerful presence in a physical way ({{Job 38:1|38:1}}; {{Nahum 1:3|Nahum 1:3}}; {{Acts 2:2|Acts 2:2}}; compare {{1 Kings 19:11|1 Kings 19:11}}).

The characters in the book often say that no one is truly *righteous* or *pure* (see {{Job 9:2|9:2}}; {{Job 15:14|15:14}}; {{Job 25:4|25:4}}; {{Job 35:7|35:7}}). This is because everyone is flawed ({{Psalm 14:3|Psalms 14:3}}; {{Psalm 53:3|53:3}}; {{Romans 3:10-11|Romans 3:10–11}}). Eliphaz used these terms to say that humans are full of sin and God has no sin. Job and God used them to show that Job had fulfilled his duties to God. Job and Eliphaz never agreed on what these terms meant. Later, God said that Eliphaz had not spoken about him "accurately" ({{Job 42:7|Job 42:7}}).
The idea that God does not *trust His servants* and *charges His angels with error* is unique (but see {{Genesis 6:1-4|Genesis 6:1–4}}).
A *tent* often symbolized human life ({{Isaiah 38:12|Isaiah 38:12}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:1|2 Corinthians 5:1}}; compare {{Ecclesiastes 12:6|Ecclesiastes 12:6}}).

*The holy ones* probably refers back to the angels mentioned in {{Job 4:18|4:18}}. They are "holy ones" because of they are close to God, not because they have achieved moral perfection ({{Job 15:15|15:15}}; {{Daniel 4:14|Daniel 4:14}}; {{Daniel 8:13|8:13}}; {{Zechariah 14:5|Zechariah 14:5}}).

*in court*: Literally this reads, *in the gate.* At that time, legal and business discussions happened. Job participated in these discussions ({{Job 29:7|29:7}}; see {{Deuteronomy 21:19-21|Deuteronomy 21:19–21}}; {{Ruth 4:1-11|Ruth 4:1–11}}).

- *Appeal to God*: This meant a formal request for help, advice, or removal of blame, sometimes through asking God to forgive ({{Amos 5:4|Amos 5:4}}, {{Amos 5:6|6}}). It could possibly refer to an *appeal *through a message from a prophet ({{Genesis 25:22|Genesis 25:22}}; {{1 Samuel 9:9|1 Samuel 9:9}}; {{1 Kings 22:8|1 Kings 22:8}}).

- Job wanted to present his *cause before God.* Later he tried to do that very thing ({{Job 13:3|Job 13:3}}, {{Job 13:15|15}}, {{Job 13:18|18}}; {{Job 23:3-8|23:3–8}}; {{Job 29:1-31:40|29:1–31:40}}).
The region where Job lived relied on *rain* instead of human methods to water crops (see {{Job 36:27-28|36:27–28}}).

Eliphaz praised God as the creator and and the one who sustains the universe who performs wonders ({{Job 5:9-10|5:9–10}}). He also praised God as the righteous judge who humbles the powerful and honors poor people ({{Job 5:11-16|5:11–16}}).

God *catches the wise in their craftiness* ({{Proverbs 12:13|Proverbs 12:13}}). The apostle Paul referred to this idea when he rejected the wisdom of the world ({{1 Corinthians 1:19|1 Corinthians 1:19}}).

- *Six calamities … in seven*: This formula for wise sayings suggests a condition of completion (compare {{Proverbs 30:15-31|Proverbs 30:15–31}}).

- This list reflects the blessings and curses of the covenant God gave to Moses ({{Leviticus 26:1-46|Leviticus 26}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:1-68|Deuteronomy 28}}). 

Eliphaz believed that people in a right relationship with God would avoid: 

- *Famine*, meaning starving. ({{Job 5:20|Job 5:20}}, {{Job 5:22|22}}; see {{Leviticus 26:4-5|Leviticus 26:4–5}}, {{Leviticus 26:10|10}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:4-6|Deuteronomy 28:4–6}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:8|8}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:11-12|11–12}}).

- *Battle* and its *destruction* ({{Job 5:20|Job 5:20}}; {{Job 5:21|5:21}}, {{Job 5:22|22}}; see {{Leviticus 26:6-8|Leviticus 26:6–8}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:7|Deuteronomy 28:7}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:48|48}}).

- *Scourge of the tongue, *or words spoken against them (slander).

- They would even be at *peace* with *wild animals *and *the stones of the field* ({{Job 5:23|Job 5:23}}; see {{Leviticus 26:6|Leviticus 26:6}}). This *peace* might mean productive fields instead of rocky ones ({{2 Kings 3:19|2 Kings 3:19}}, {{2 Kings 3:25|25}}; {{Matthew 13:5|Matthew 13:5}}). Or it might symbolize broader harmony with creation (see {{Psalm 91:11-12|Psalm 91:11–12}}).
*descendants like the grass of the earth*: See {{Genesis 22:17|Genesis 22:17}}; {{Leviticus 26:9|Leviticus 26:9}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:4|Deuteronomy 28:4}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:11-12|11–12}}.

Job responds by criticizing his counselors and questioning God (chapters {{Job 6:1-30|6}}and {{Job 7:1-21|7}}). He explains his intense words by indicating his deep "grief" or "anguish" ({{Job 6:2-3|6:2–3}}; {{Job 7:11|7:11}}). Job states that Eliphaz has not provided comfort or sympathy as a friend. Instead, Eliphaz chose to argue about out of date religious or theological ideas.

In the Old Testament, *arrows* symbolize danger, disease, and destruction from God ({{Job 7:20|7:20}}; {{Job 16:12-13|16:12–13}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:23-24|Deuteronomy 32:23–24}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:42|42}}; {{Psalm 7:12-13|Psalms 7:12–13}}; {{Psalm 38:2|38:2}}; {{Psalm 64:7|64:7}}; {{Psalm 91:5-6|91:5–6}}; {{Lamentations 2:4|Lamentations 2:4}}; {{Lamentations 3:12-13|3:12–13}}; {{Ezekiel 5:16|Ezekiel 5:16}}).

*The tasteless food … the white of an egg?* Job's complaint in the form of a word puzzle (riddle) probably refers to both Eliphaz's weak advice and the situation God allowed him to endure that Job hates.
At one time, both the prophets Moses and Elijah asked God to end their lives ({{Numbers 11:15|Numbers 11:15}}; {{1 Kings 19:4|1 Kings 19:4}}).

Job and his friends might have shared a covenant (special agreement) of loyalty and faith (Hebrew *khesed*; see {{Genesis 21:23|Genesis 21:23}}; {{Exodus 15:13|Exodus 15:13}}; {{1 Chronicles 16:34|1 Chronicles 16:34}}). This bond would have made them like brothers, those who protect, and friends he could trust ({{Job 6:14-15|Job 6:14–15}}; {{Job 6:21-23|6:21–23,}}{{Job 6:27|27}}). If they were in a covenant with one another, Job was accusing his friends of violating their covenant with him.

- The city of *Tema*, located in the northern Arabian desert, was at the place roads crossed from Damascus to Mecca and from the Persian Gulf to Aqaba ({{Isaiah 21:14|Isaiah 21:14}}; {{Jeremiah 25:23|Jeremiah 25:23}}). They might have named it after an ancestor who descended from Ishmael ({{Genesis 25:15|Genesis 25:15}}). It was different from "Teman," which was Eliphaz’s home in Edom.

- *Sheba*, situated in southwest Arabia, was a trading city for valuable goods ({{Psalm 72:10|Psalm 72:10}}, {{Psalm 72:15|15}}; {{Isaiah 60:6|Isaiah 60:6}}; {{Jeremiah 6:20|Jeremiah 6:20}}; {{Ezekiel 27:22-23|Ezekiel 27:22–23}}; {{Ezekiel 38:13|38:13}}).

*even cast lots for an orphan*: Job once protected orphans ({{Job 31:17|31:17}}, {{Job 31:21|21}}). He used a common saying to show his counselors' lack of compassion for those who had no one to defend them (see {{Job 17:5|17:5}}).
*Can my mouth not discern malice?*: Job might have been referring to his earlier comment about a "tasteless" and unpleasant diet ({{Job 6:6-7|6:6–7}}).

Human life has been difficult since the effects of the first human sin ({{Genesis 3:17|Genesis 3:17}}; {{Genesis 5:29|5:29}}; {{Ecclesiastes 1:2|Ecclesiastes 1:2}}, {{Ecclesiastes 1:13-14|13–14}}; {{Ecclesiastes 2:11|2:11}}, {{Ecclesiastes 2:17|17}}; {{Romans 8:20-22|Romans 8:20–22}}).

Employers had the obligation to pay workers at the end of each day ({{Leviticus 19:13|Leviticus 19:13}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:15|Deuteronomy 24:15}}). But this did not always happen ({{Jeremiah 22:13|Jeremiah 22:13}}; {{Malachi 3:5|Malachi 3:5}}; {{James 5:4|James 5:4}}).

- Job's testing might have lasted for months. 

- The Hebrew word (*'amal*) appears throughout Job and means "*misery*" or "miserable" or "trouble" ({{Job 3:20|3:20}}; {{Job 11:16|11:16}}; {{Job 16:2|16:2}}; {{Job 20:22|20:22}}; {{Job 3:10|3:10}}; {{Job 4:8|4:8}}; {{Job 5:6|5:6}}, {{Job 5:7|7}}; {{Job 15:35|15:35}}).

Job's mention of *worms* symbolized the human fate of death and the widespread corruption in Sheol ({{Job 25:6|25:6}}; {{Job 17:14|17:14}}; {{Job 21:26|21:26}}; {{Job 24:20|24:20}}; see {{Isaiah 14:11|Isaiah 14:11}}).
Job cried out to God, saying life was too short ({{Job 7:6-10|7:6–10}}). This complaint contrasts with his earlier wish for God to end his life ({{Job 6:9|6:9}}).

- People who ask God to *remember* usually seek his promised mercy ({{Psalm 35:6|Psalms 35:6}}; {{Psalm 106:4|106:4}}).

- Job's statement that life is *but a breath* (Hebrew *ruakh*) meant he was either close to death or that life is like the passing of the wind ({{Psalm 39:9|Psalm 39:9}}, {{Psalm 39:11|11}}).

*You will look for me, but I will be no more*: The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) left out this verse. They did not want to suggest that God could not see Job in Sheol (see study note on 7:9).

*goes down to Sheol*: This is the first plain mention of Sheol in Job. 

It is described as: 

- A place of rest from the pressures and distinctions of earth ({{Job 3:13-19|3:13–19}}).

- "Darkness" ({{Job 10:21-22|10:21–22}}; {{Job 17:13|17:13}}).

- Deep in the earth ({{Job 11:8|11:8}}).

- Covered in dust ({{Job 17:16|17:16}}). 

- The fate of all living beings from which no one can return ({{Job 30:23|30:23}}; {{Job 10:21|10:21}}; see {{Genesis 37:25|Genesis 37:25}}; {{2 Samuel 12:12|2 Samuel 12:12}}).
*I will not restrain my mouth*: Job echoed Eliphaz's struggle to "keep from speaking" ({{Job 4:2|4:2}}).

*The sea* (Hebrew *yam*) and *the monster* (Hebrew *tannin*) symbolize chaos opposing God's order of creation. In Canaanite mythology, "Yam" was the original *sea* god, and "Tannin" was a sea *monster* or a god of the myth of chaos ({{Jeremiah 51:34|Jeremiah 51:34}}; {{Psalm 74:13-14|Psalm 74:13–14}}). This chaos also appears in Job as "Leviathan" or "Rahab" ({{Job 3:8|Job 3:8}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}; {{Job 9:13|Job 9:13}}; {{Job 26:12|26:12}}; {{Isaiah 51:9|Isaiah 51:9}}). The Lord has total control (sovereignty) over the *sea* and everything it represents ({{Job 26:12|Job 26:12}}; {{Job 38:8-11|38:8–11}}; {{Psalm 89:9-10|Psalm 89:9–10}}; {{Jeremiah 5:22|Jeremiah 5:22}}).
Job's *dreams* and *visions* while sick were similar to those of Eliphaz ({{Job 4:12-16|4:12–16}}).
*for my days are but a breath*: Literally *for my days are a vapor* (Hebrew *hebel*); see the Theme Note titled “All Is ‘Vapor’.”

- *that You should exalt him*: Compare with {{Psalm 8:4-5|Psalm 8:4–5}}, which expresses similar thoughts in a positive way. 

- *attend *(Hebrew *paqad*): In {{Psalm 8:4|Psalm 8:4}}, this term means "to honor or care for." Job used it ironically to mean "You bother yourself" (compare with "punished," {{Isaiah 26:14|Isaiah 26:14}}).

- *Will You never look away from me* (literally *How long will you not look away from me*): Job wanted the opposite of the attention that loyal people usually desire ({{Numbers 6:25|Numbers 6:25}}; {{Psalm 27:9|Psalms 27:9}}; {{Psalm 69:17|69:17}}; {{Psalm 80:3|80:3}}, {{Psalm 80:7|7}}, {{Psalm 80:19|19}}; {{Lamentations 1:9|Lamentations 1:9}}).

- *to swallow*: This means “a chance to calm my breathing.”

- *Watcher of mankind*: Instead of praising God for his goodness shown in careful attention, Job accused God of hostile surveillance. This actually describes Satan's actions ({{Deuteronomy 32:10|Deuteronomy 32:10}}; {{Psalm 25:21|Psalm 25:21}}; {{Proverbs 24:12|Proverbs 24:12}}; {{Job 1:7|Job 1:7}}).

- *Why* comes from the language of grief (see study note on 3:11–24). 

- *Your target*: See {{Job 6:4|6:4}}; {{Lamentations 3:12|Lamentations 3:12}}.

Like Eliphaz, *Bildad the Shuhite* thought Job's suffering was God's punishment (see study note on 2:11; {{Job 8:3-6|8:3–6}}, {{Job 8:13|13}}; compare {{Job 4:7-8|4:7–8}}; {{Job 5:2-3|5:2–3}}). *Bildad* respected the wisdom of the past and spoke to Job with both advice and encouragement ({{Job 8:8-10|8:8–10}}; compare {{Job 4:7|4:7}}; {{Job 8:3-6|8:3–6}}, {{Job 8:8-10|8–10}}; compare {{Job 4:12-21|4:12–21}}; {{Job 5:9-16|5:9–16}}; {{Job 8:5-7|8:5–7}}, {{Job 8:20-22|20–22}}; compare {{Job 4:6|4:6}}; {{Job 5:19-26|5:19–26}}). He suggested that Job should stop complaining. *Bildad* advised Job to "ask the Almighty for mercy" and let God's justice restore him ({{Job 8:1-7|8:1–7}}).
*How long*: Bildad might have meant make fun of Job using a similar question (see {{Job 7:19|7:19}}).

Bildad believed God does not *pervert justice*. He thought the death of Job’s children showed they had *sinned* against God. Bildad divided people into "the blameless" (Hebrew *tam*, {{Job 8:20|8:20a}}; see {{Job 1:1|1:1}}) or "the godless" (Hebrew *khanep*, {{Job 8:13|8:13b}}). He believed one could distinguish them by observing God's actions toward them.
*your latter days will flourish*: Bildad's words were more accurate than he realized ({{Job 42:12|42:12}}; compare {{Job 5:19-26|5:19–26}}).
Bildad argued for traditional wisdom by referring to ancient traditions and history ({{Deuteronomy 4:32|Deuteronomy 4:32}}; {{Jeremiah 18:13|Jeremiah 18:13}}).
*born yesterday and know nothing*: Bildad suggested that Job's generation was either born too late to know ancient wisdom or too young to have gathered it.
*Papyrus* reeds can grow as high as three to four and one-half meters (ten to fifteen feet).

To *forget God* means behaving as if God does not exist or cannot see (see {{Psalm 10:4|Psalms 10:4}}; {{Psalm 14:1|14:1}}; {{Zephaniah 1:12|Zephaniah 1:12}}; see {{Job 22:13-17|Job 22:13–17}}; {{Psalm 94:7|Psalm 94:7}}).
In this symbolic story, a *plant* spreads *its shoots over the garden*. The *roots wrap around the rock heap*, giving the plant stability.

*Job answered *Bildad by describing God's universal and legal power. His speech resembles a complex legal case. 

It includes: 

- A summons and response ({{Job 9:3|9:3}}, {{Job 9:14-16|14–16}}, {{Job 9:19|19b}}, {{Job 9:32|32}}).

- The risk of proving himself guilty ({{Job 9:20|9:20}}).

- A "mediator" ({{Job 9:33-34|9:33–34}}).

- A question of accusation ({{Job 9:12|9:12}}).

- A legal sentence ({{Job 9:22|9:22}}).

- A declaration of guilt ({{Job 9:28-30|9:28–30}}).
*If one wished to contend with God*: Job later wished to meet God in court ({{Job 13:3|13:3}}, {{Job 13:15|15}}, {{Job 13:23|23}}; {{Job 23:4|23:4}}).

When God *moves mountains* or *shakes the earth*, it shows his presence as:

- One who gives laws ({{Exodus 19:18|Exodus 19:18}}).

- One who judges ({{Jeremiah 4:24|Jeremiah 4:24}}).

- One who rescues ({{Psalm 18:7|Psalm 18:7}}; {{Isaiah 13:13|Isaiah 13:13}}; {{Isaiah 29:6|29:6}}).

- {{Job 38:32|Job 38:32}}mentions *the Bear. *It is often identified as "Arcturus." It might also refer to the *constellations *(star patterns) "Ursa Minor" or "Leo." 

- *the Pleiades* is a group of seven stars, referenced at {{Job 38:31|38:31}} and {{Amos 5:8|Amos 5:8}}.

*the helpers of Rahab*: Job described the power of demons as mythical sea monsters that represented chaos. This kind of imagery appears in other parts of the Bible as well ({{Job 26:12|26:12}}; {{Psalm 89:11|Psalm 89:11}}; {{Isaiah 51:9|Isaiah 51:9}}).
*with a tempest*: The words translated as “with a tempest” (*bis’arah*) might also mean *besa‘arah* (“for a hair,” meaning “for the smallest thing”). This would parallel "*without cause*."
Job was truly *blameless*, and he consistently claimed this during the debate ({{Job 1:1|1:1}}, {{Job 1:7|7}}; {{Job 2:3|2:3}}; {{Job 23:11-12|23:11–12}}; {{Job 27:5|27:5}}; {{Job 31:1-40|31:1–40}}).
The word "*You*" shows this is a prayer, even though, "O God," is not plainly stated in Hebrew.
*wash myself*: Job talked about using the strongest soap (*lye*) to represent removing all sin ({{Job 1:5|1:5}}; compare {{Psalm 26:6|Psalm 26:6}}; {{Matthew 27:24|Matthew 27:24}}).

- *The pit *can refer to the place of dead people, suggesting the "corruption" of death ({{Job 17:14|17:14}}; {{Job 33:18|33:18}}).

- The dirty *clothes* representing being guilty contrast with the clean *clothes* representing being innocent ({{Zechariah 3:3-5|Zechariah 3:3–5}}; see {{Isaiah 61:10|Isaiah 61:10}}; {{Isaiah 64:6|64:6}}; {{Revelation 19:8|Revelation 19:8}}).
*A mediator* does not judge God and man. Instead, the *mediator* helps bring them together (see {{Job 16:19-21|16:19–21}}).

- A series of images shows God's role in creating Job. 

- *Your hands shaped me … You molded me like clay*: This is how a "potter" makes a vessel ({{Isaiah 45:9|Isaiah 45:9}}; {{Jeremiah 18:1-12|Jeremiah 18:1–12}}). Although the potter has complete control over the *clay*, Job still questioned God ({{Isaiah 45:9|Isaiah 45:9}}; {{Jeremiah 18:5-12|Jeremiah 18:5–12}}; {{Romans 9:20-25|Romans 9:20–25}}).

- *return me to dust*: This common theme in Job shows life's temporary nature ({{Job 4:19|Job 4:19}}; {{Job 7:9-10|7:9–10}}, {{Job 7:21|21}}; {{Job 14:1-2|14:1–2}}, {{Job 14:10|10}}; see {{Genesis 3:19|Genesis 3:19}}).

- *You not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese*: The Hebrew terms create a lively image of a new born baby still covered with vernix (a creamy substance).
Earlier, Job described "Sheol" as a somewhat peaceful place ({{Job 3:13-19|3:13–19}}). Now, he calls it *a land of darkness and gloom* (see also {{Job 7:9-10|7:9–10}}; {{Job 14:7-22|14:7–22}}).
*Zophar the Naamathite*, the most harsh of Job’s three friends, focused only on the issue of sin (see study note on 2:11).

- *This stream of words*: Those who are foolish and those who sin often talk too much, but Job was innocent ({{Proverbs 10:8|Proverbs 10:8}}, {{Job 10:14|14}}; {{Proverbs 10:19|Proverbs 10:19}}).

- *Will you scoff without rebuke?*: Zophar thought Job's comments were full of sin because he was making fun of God's justice ({{Job 10:2-7|Job 10:2–7}}, {{Job 10:13-15|13–15}}).
*My doctrine is sound*: Job was not defining doctrine but was defending his own integrity.
*exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves*: Zophar believed that disasters were God's punishment for sins (compare {{Job 34:36|34:36}}).
*discover the limits of the Almighty*: No one can fully understand *the Almighty*, who is beyond the heavens, the place of dead people, the land, and the sea ({{Job 11:8-9|11:8–9}}).

Zophar outlined three conditions for restoration ({{Job 11:15|11:15}}): 

- *Direct your heart.* This is an internal action beyond mere ceremony.

- *Lift up your hands. *This is a symbolic gesture of prayer, appeal, or act of surrendering ({{Exodus 9:29|Exodus 9:29}}; {{Proverbs 1:24|Proverbs 1:24}}; {{Isaiah 1:15|Isaiah 1:15}}).

- *Put away the iniquity.* This is not through sacrifice and regret, but by quitting the sin in view (compare {{Hebrews 11:6|Hebrews 11:6}}; {{James 4:8|James 4:8}}; {{James 5:16|5:16}}).
In his longest speech so far, Job responds to Zophar's comments and the entire first round of speeches.

*ask the animals … the birds … the earth … the fish*: Job believed the reason for his grief was obvious and that even creation would understand it ({{Proverbs 6:6|Proverbs 6:6}}). Later, God directed Job to the animal kingdom to show him that he did not understand ({{Job 38:1-40:24|Job 38–40}}).
The change from *you* (plural in {{Job 12:2-3|12:2–3}}) to *you* (singular here) probably indicates that Job is speaking to Zophar.

*the hand of the LORD*: This is the only place in the dialogues where the Hebrew name, "Yahweh" (“the LORD”), appears (chapters {{Job 3:1-27:23|3–27}}; {{Job 29:1-37:24|29–37}}). For Job, the issue was not who caused his grief but why it happened.

*Wisdom is found with the elderly: *People often think *wisdom* comes with old age. Job's friends supported this idea but Job doubted it ({{Job 8:8-10|8:8–10}}; {{Job 15:10|15:10}}; {{Job 32:6-9|32:6–9}}; {{Job 12:20|12:20}}).
*He leads counselors away barefoot*: In this metaphor, God removes leaders' abilities. It could also mean losing the symbols of office or becoming naked captives ({{Job 12:18-19|12:18–19}}).

When God removes the royal robe of kings, he takes away their symbols of authority (compare {{Job 19:9|19:9}}). It can also mean "God loosens the bonds of kings," referring to the control they have imposed on others.
The *priests* lose their status or their priestly robes. They might even be naked captives ({{Job 12:18|12:18}}).

- *Pours out contempt on nobles*: Compare {{Psalm 107:40|Psalm 107:40}}.

- *disarms the mighty* (literally *loosens the belt of*): The strong are not ready for battle anymore.

- *He reveals the deep things*: This phrase might refer to Zophar’s words that God’s knowledge is "deeper than Sheol" ({{Job 11:8|11:8}}). 

- *darkness … deep shadows*: The Old Testament often describes God as living in *darkness* and showing himself through *darkness* ({{1 Kings 8:12|1 Kings 8:12}}; {{2 Chronicles 6:1|2 Chronicles 6:1}}; {{2 Samuel 22:10|2 Samuel 22:10}}, {{2 Samuel 22:12|12}}; {{Psalm 18:9|Psalm 18:9}}, {{Psalm 18:11|11}}). Examples are when he gave the law at Sinai or when he comes in judgment ({{Deuteronomy 4:11|Deuteronomy 4:11}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:22-23|5:22–23}}; {{Zephaniah 1:15|Zephaniah 1:15}}).

- Compare {{Daniel 2:21|Daniel 2:21}}. 

- *He deprives the earth’s leaders of reason*: See {{Job 12:18|Job 12:18}}; compare {{Daniel 4:23|Daniel 4:23}}, {{Daniel 4:32-33|32–33}}. 

- *He… makes them wander in a trackless wasteland*: This is like the "nobles" in {{Psalm 107:40|Psalm 107:40}} (see {{Job 12:21|Job 12:21}}).

Lack of wise advice might have caused the kings to *stagger like drunkards* ({{Job 12:17|12:17}}; see {{Isaiah 19:14|Isaiah 19:14}}). This happened because they experienced God's punishment ({{Psalm 75:8|Psalm 75:8}}; {{Jeremiah 25:15-27|Jeremiah 25:15–27}}).
Job appealed to experience, just like his comforters had done ({{Job 3:12-17|3:12–17}}; {{Job 5:2|5:2}}).
*Will you speak wickedly on God’s behalf*: False witnesses were not allowed, even when speaking for God ({{Exodus 20:16|Exodus 20:16}}).
Job thought about finding a judge to remove God's burden from him ({{Job 9:33-34|9:33–34}}). Eliphaz had encouraged Job to accept God's discipline ({{Job 5:17|5:17}}).

Job wanted God to *call* or summon him, so Job could defend himself. Or as an alternative, Job would *speak* to God. Then God would respond with the charges against Job. Since God did not choose the first option, Job started the second one ({{Job 13:23|13:23}}). Eventually, God did *call* Job ({{Job 38:1-3|38:1–3}}; {{Job 40:1-2|40:1–2}}). But Job could not *reply* ({{Job 40:3-5|40:3–5}}).

- God can turn away in "anger"({{Deuteronomy 31:18|Deuteronomy 31:18}}; {{Isaiah 54:8|Isaiah 54:8}}; {{Jeremiah 33:5|Jeremiah 33:5}}). Or he can choose not to show friendship ({{Psalm 30:7|Psalms 30:7}}; {{Psalm 69:17|69:17}}; {{Psalm 102:2|102:2}}).

- Job, perhaps making a play of words on his own name (*’iyyob*), denied being God's *enemy* (*’oyeb*).

In the Old Testament, *dry chaff* often symbolizes something that can blow away or burn ({{Psalm 83:13|Psalm 83:13}}; {{Isaiah 40:24|Isaiah 40:24}}; {{Jeremiah 13:24|Jeremiah 13:24}}; {{Exodus 15:7|Exodus 15:7}}; {{Isaiah 47:14|Isaiah 47:14}}; {{Malachi 4:1|Malachi 4:1}}; see also “dry grass,” {{Isaiah 5:24|Isaiah 5:24}}; {{Isaiah 33:11|33:11}}). It also represents weakness and lack of importance ({{Job 41:20-21|Job 41:20–21}}; {{Isaiah 41:2|Isaiah 41:2}}).

- The *flower* symbolizes how short life is ({{Psalm 90:5-6|Psalms 90:5–6}}; {{Psalm 103:15-16|103:15–16}}; {{Isaiah 40:6-7|Isaiah 40:6–7}}). 

- A *shadow* passes quickly ({{1 Chronicles 29:15|1 Chronicles 29:15}}; {{Psalm 102:11|Psalm 102:11}}).
*open Your eyes*: Job complained about God's constant surveillance ({{Job 7:8|7:8}}, {{Job 7:17-20|17–20}}; {{Job 10:6|10:6}}, {{Job 10:14|14}}; {{Job 13:27|13:27}}).

*does not rise: *Job did not have even the minimal evidence of resurrection found in the Old Testament ({{2 Kings 13:21|2 Kings 13:21}}; {{Isaiah 26:19|Isaiah 26:19}}; {{Daniel 12:2|Daniel 12:2}}; see also {{Job 19:25|Job 19:25}}). Job was not focusing on the end of the universe when the heavens will disappear ({{Psalm 102:25-26|Psalm 102:25–26}}; {{Isaiah 34:4|Isaiah 34:4}}; {{Isaiah 51:6|51:6}}; {{Hebrews 1:10-12|Hebrews 1:10–12}}). He was referring to the eternal nature of *the heavens* ({{Psalm 148:6|Psalm 148:6}}; see also {{Psalm 72:5|Psalms 72:5}}, {{Psalm 72:7|7}}, {{Psalm 72:17|17}}; {{Psalm 89:29|89:29}}, {{Psalm 89:37|37}}). His phrase refers to the permanent state of death.

The grave is a permanent home ({{Job 14:10-12|14:10–12}}, see {{Job 3:13-19|3:13–19}}; {{Job 7:6-10|7:6–10}}; {{Job 10:20-22|10:20–22}}). Job could not fulfill his request from {{Job 13:20-21|13:20–21}} to *hide* temporarily in the grave.
*count my steps*: Here, Job refers to God's protective care rather than his surveillance ({{Job 10:12|10:12}}; {{Job 13:27|13:27}}; {{Job 14:3|14:3}}).

If *transgression* becomes *sealed* in a bag, it does not wait for judgment ({{Deuteronomy 32:34-35|Deuteronomy 32:34–35}}; {{Hosea 13:12|Hosea 13:12}}). It remains hidden forever. Job was asking for God to forgive him.

Job no longer considered Sheol as a safe place ({{Job 3:17-19|3:17–19}}; {{Job 14:13-17|14:13–17}}). The Old Testament often describes dead people as having no feelings ({{Psalm 88:12|Psalm 88:12}}; {{Ecclesiastes 9:5|Ecclesiastes 9:5}}; compare {{Isaiah 50:11|Isaiah 50:11}}; {{Isaiah 66:24|66:24}}). The New Testament more plainly teaches that evil dead people experience suffering ({{Luke 16:23|Luke 16:23}}, {{Luke 16:28|28}}; {{Revelation 14:11|Revelation 14:11}}).
In this second round of speeches, Job's friends discuss the fate of wicked people. They suggest that Job's condition means he has sinned.

*fill his belly with the hot east wind*: The *east wind* was hot, so it might symbolize upset or violent speech ({{Exodus 14:21|Exodus 14:21}}; {{Hosea 13:15|Hosea 13:15}}; {{Jonah 4:8|Jonah 4:8}}; {{Job 27:21|Job 27:21}}; {{Jeremiah 18:17|Jeremiah 18:17}}).
*Your own mouth … condemns you*: Job feared this would happen ({{Job 9:20|9:20}}; see {{Matthew 26:65|Matthew 26:65}}).
When the Lord later gave a similar challenge, Job found it convincing ({{Job 38:1-11|38:1–11}}).

The book's readers know about God's secret *council* ({{Job 1:6-12|1:6–12}}; {{Job 2:1-6|2:1–6}}; see {{1 Kings 22:19-20|1 Kings 22:19–20}}; {{Psalm 89:5-7|Psalm 89:5–7}}). But Job and his friends did not.
*Aged* men who are *gray-haired* claim they alone have wisdom ({{Job 8:8-10|8:8–10}}; {{Job 12:20|12:20}}; see {{Job 12:2|12:2}}).
*why do your eyes flash*: This sentence might be a metaphor for unbelief, or it could mean winking like a person planning a trick or someone blinking in disbelief.

- *What is man, that he should be pure*: Eliphaz repeated himself and Job ({{Job 4:17-19|4:17–19}}; {{Job 7:17|7:17}}; {{Job 14:4|14:4}}).

- *one born of woman*: Both *man *and *born of woman* suggest weakness.
The heavens, often linked with what is *pure*, were not completely *pure* ({{Exodus 24:10|Exodus 24:10}}). Rebellious angels may have brought pollution ({{Job 1:6-7|Job 1:6–7}}).
*when no foreigner passed among them*: Eliphaz's contempt for foreign ideas is ironic. Wisdom literature is more international than other Old Testament writings.

Evil people experience everything that happened to Job (see {{Job 1:16-19|1:16–19}}):

- Attacks by thieves ({{Job 15:21|15:21}}).

- Loss of possessions ({{Job 15:29|15:29}}).

- Collapse of houses ({{Job 15:28|15:28}}).

- Fire ({{Job 15:30|15:30}}, {{Job 15:34|34}}).

- Eliphaz spoke about the fear that evil people feel, and Job had similar experiences ({{Job 3:25|3:25}}; {{Job 6:4|6:4}}; {{Job 9:34|9:34}}; {{Job 13:11|13:11}}, {{Job 13:21|21}}; {{Job 23:15|23:15}}; {{Job 27:20|27:20}}; {{Job 30:15|30:15}}). Bildad and Zophar warned of more fear to come ({{Job 18:11|18:11,14}}{{Job 18:14|;}}{{Job 20:25|20:25}}). 

- The Sabeans and Chaldeans were examples of "destroyers" ({{Job 1:13-17|1:13–17}}). But this could mean any destructive force ({{Job 1:18-19|1:18–19}}). A *destroyer *might be an agent of Satan or divine agents that punish evil ({{1 Corinthians 10:10|1 Corinthians 10:10}}; {{Revelation 9:11|Revelation 9:11}}; {{Exodus 12:23|Exodus 12:23}}; {{2 Samuel 24:16|2 Samuel 24:16}}; {{2 Chronicles 32:21|2 Chronicles 32:21}}; {{Acts 12:23|Acts 12:23}}; {{Hebrews 11:28|Hebrews 11:28}}). Eliphaz referred to divine agents.
*he is marked for the sword*: The evil people may die by murder or by God's punishment.

Like evil people, Job may have experienced hunger. Or, following the ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), the Berean Standard Bible says Job "wanders about as food for vultures.” This would be similar to being “marked for the sword” ({{Job 15:22|15:22}}).
Earlier, Job complained that God was treating him like a powerful enemy ({{Job 7:19-21|7:19–21}}; {{Job 13:24|13:24}}).

- *The flame*, could refer to the sun burning or *the flame *of judgment from God (see {{Job 15:34|15:34}}; {{Numbers 16:31-35|Numbers 16:31–35}}; {{Psalm 106:17-18|Psalms 106:17–18}}; {{Ezekiel 20:47|Ezekiel 20:47}}). 

- *the breath of God's mouth*: This might be a desert wind or a direct "theophany" (a revelation of God’s presence) that caused the "fire" of {{Job 15:34|Job 15:34}}.
"The flame" of judgment will destroy the unfair profits of those without faith ({{Job 15:30|15:30}}).

Job might have wanted to *shake* his *head* in to make fun or in horror ({{2 Kings 19:21|2 Kings 19:21}}; {{Psalm 22:7|Psalms 22:7}}; {{Psalm 109:25|109:25}}; {{Isaiah 37:22|Isaiah 37:22}}; {{Jeremiah 18:16|Jeremiah 18:16}}; {{Lamentations 2:15|Lamentations 2:15}}; {{Matthew 27:39|Matthew 27:39}}).
Job's family includes by extension his household and his servants ({{Job 1:15-19|1:15–19}}).

- *They open their mouths against me*: Job was mocked (compare {{Psalm 35:21|Psalm 35:21}}; {{Isaiah 57:4|Isaiah 57:4}}; {{Lamentations 2:16|Lamentations 2:16}}; {{Lamentations 3:46|3:46}}).

- *strike my cheeks*: This was more of an insult than an act of violence ({{Psalm 3:7|Psalm 3:7}}; {{Micah 5:1|Micah 5:1}}; see also {{1 Kings 22:24|1 Kings 22:24}}; {{Isaiah 50:6|Isaiah 50:6}}; {{Lamentations 3:30|Lamentations 3:30}}; {{Matthew 26:67|Matthew 26:67}}).

*He seized me by the neck*: This might refer to a wild animal capturing its prey (see {{Job 16:9|16:9}}). However, it is more likely a military image signaling defeat ({{Genesis 49:8|Genesis 49:8}}; {{Psalm 18:40|Psalm 18:40}}).
*my gall*: This describes injuries to important organs.

*He breaks me with wound upon wound*: Job imagines himself as a defensive military station with God attacking. Job regarded God as a warrior who neither defended nor saved him (see {{Exodus 15:3|Exodus 15:3}}; {{Psalm 24:8|Psalm 24:8}}; see {{Jeremiah 20:11|Jeremiah 20:11}}; {{Zephaniah 3:17|Zephaniah 3:17}}). Instead, God attacked him as if he were a threat (see {{Job 6:12|Job 6:12}}; {{Isaiah 42:13|Isaiah 42:13}}).

- Since Job insisted he was innocent, wearing *sackcloth* showed grief, not asking God to forgive him. He might have worn it to show he would never take it off because no one could comfort him ({{Genesis 37:34-35|Genesis 37:34–35}}).

- *I have buried my horn in the dust*: A *horn* symbolized dignity and power ({{1 Samuel 2:1|1 Samuel 2:1}}; {{Psalm 75:4-5|Psalms 75:4–5}}; {{Psalm 89:17|89:17}}, {{Psalm 89:24|24}}; {{Psalm 92:10|92:10}}; {{Psalm 112:9|112:9}}; {{Psalm 148:14|148:14}}). Cutting it off caused deep humiliation ({{Psalm 75:10|Psalm 75:10}}; {{Jeremiah 48:25|Jeremiah 48:25}}; {{Zechariah 1:12|Zechariah 1:12}}).

- *Free of violence *(Hebrew *lo’-khamas*): If *violence* is the meaning, Job might have been denying that he was a dangerous warrior who God should attack ({{Job 16:12-14|16:12–14}}; see also {{Isaiah 59:6|Isaiah 59:6}}; {{Jonah 3:8|Jonah 3:8}}).

- Contrary to Eliphaz’s accusation and Bildad’s assumption, Job’s prayer was sincere because he was innocent ({{Job 15:4-5|Job 15:4–5}}; {{Job 8:6|8:6}}; {{Genesis 20:5|Genesis 20:5}}; {{Isaiah 59:3|Isaiah 59:3}}).
Job's *blood* would testify that he was innocent and suffered without cause (compare {{Genesis 4:10-11|Genesis 4:10–11}}; {{Isaiah 26:21|Isaiah 26:21}}; {{Ezekiel 24:7-8|Ezekiel 24:7–8}}).
Job thought his suffering would lead to his death ({{Job 7:7|7:7}}, {{Job 7:21|21}}; {{Job 10:20-22|10:20–22}}). He asked God to show his innocence, even if he died before that happened.

*my witness is in heaven*: Job wished for a kind third party to be "a mediator" between him and God (see {{Job 9:32-35|9:32–35}}). Job wanted a heavenly *advocate* who would eventually stand on the earth ({{Job 16:19|16:19}}; compare {{Zechariah 3:1|Zechariah 3:1}}; {{Job 19:25|Job 19:25}}; compare {{1 Samuel 24:15|1 Samuel 24:15}}; {{John 14:16|John 14:16}}, {{John 14:26|26}}; {{John 15:26|15:26}}; {{John 16:7|16:7}}; {{1 John 2:1|1 John 2:1}}).
*My spirit is broken*: This can mean a truly sorry attitude ({{Psalm 51:17|Psalm 51:17}}). But it usually means a very sad "spirit" ({{Proverbs 18:14|Proverbs 18:14}}).

*mockers surround me*: songs of grief (laments) often describe making fun of someone as how evil people respond to the suffering of righteous people ({{Psalm 22:7|Psalms 22:7}}; {{Psalm 69:10-12|69:10–12}}; {{Psalm 89:50-52|89:50–52}}). In wisdom literature, people make fun of right behavior ({{Proverbs 1:22|Proverbs 1:22}}; {{Proverbs 9:7|9:7}}).

*Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand *(literally *please keep my pledge with yourself*): A *pledge* (Hebrew *‘erabon*) can be a deposit that guarantees payment ({{Genesis 38:17-20|Genesis 38:17–20}}; {{Exodus 22:26-27|Exodus 22:26–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:10-14|Deuteronomy 24:10–14}}; see {{Proverbs 20:16|Proverbs 20:16}}; {{Proverbs 27:13|27:13}}). So, this might suggest God forgiving sin (making atonement). It might also refer to Job’s wish for an advocate to support his cause (see study note on Job 16:19–21).
Spitting in someone's face was more insulting than a slap because it made the person ceremonially unclean ({{Job 16:10|16:10}}; {{Numbers 12:14|Numbers 12:14}}).
Some scholars think these verses are out of place. However, Job might have been quoting his opponents' words ironically.
Job no longer trusted his friends and thought he would die without hope ({{Job 6:15-21|6:15–21}}; {{Job 13:4-5|13:4–5}}; {{Job 16:2-3|16:2–3}}; compare {{Job 12:2|12:2}}).
*for Sheol*: People imagined the realm of dead people as a *home* ({{Job 30:23|30:23}}; {{Psalm 49:11|Psalm 49:11}}; {{Ecclesiastes 12:5|Ecclesiastes 12:5}}).
*my father … mother … sister*: This sad imitation of a family gathering in a cemetery shows how Job imagined his coming death.
*the gates of Sheol: Sheol *is the place where dead people reside. Ancient people thought it had a gate with bars that allowed no escape.
*How long until you end these speeches?*: Bildad spoke to Job as if addressing a group, possibly meaning "people like you."

The phrase, "the lamp of the wicked is extinguished," might symbolize a life filled with confusion and darkness ({{Proverbs 4:19|Proverbs 4:19}}). More likely, it suggests an early death ({{Proverbs 13:9|Proverbs 13:9}}; {{Proverbs 24:20|24:20}}).
A *shortened stride* is the opposite of walking and running in a life of blessings ({{Proverbs 4:12|Proverbs 4:12}}).
A series of devices for hunting shows the biblical principle of revenge (see study note on 34:11).
Bildad uses the biblical idea of revenge (consequences for doing wrong) in Job's case, as do Eliphaz and Zophar.
*death devours*: The prophet Isaiah later changed this image. He pictured the Lord as defeating *death* ({{Isaiah 25:8|Isaiah 25:8}}; see {{1 Corinthians 15:54|1 Corinthians 15:54}}).

The image of *burning sulfur* reminds the reader of what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah ({{Genesis 19:24|Genesis 19:24}}). It suggests what will happen to all evil people ({{Psalm 11:6|Psalm 11:6}}; {{Revelation 19:20|Revelation 19:20}}; {{Revelation 21:8|21:8}}).

People often speak against (curse) evil people by saying that future generations will forget their *memory* (see {{Job 18:19|18:19}}; {{Psalm 34:16|Psalms 34:16}}; {{Psalm 109:13|109:13}}; {{Proverbs 10:7|Proverbs 10:7}}).

This bad fortune (curse) of Job no longer having children and Bildad’s earlier cruel acts show that he believed Job's suffering was a fair punishment because he did wrong (see {{Job 18:16|18:16}}; {{Psalm 109:13|Psalms 109:13}}; {{Isaiah 14:21-22|Isaiah 14:21–22}}; {{Job 8:4|Job 8:4}}; {{Job 1:18-19|1:18–19}}).
*in the west … in the east*: These phrases might refer to people from the past and future or from different places.
Bildad kept implying that Job had rejected God ({{Job 15:4|15:4}}, {{Job 15:13|13}}, {{Job 15:25|25}}).

The number *ten* symbolized a large, non-definite quantity rather than a specific count (for example, {{Genesis 31:7|Genesis 31:7}}; {{Leviticus 26:26|Leviticus 26:26}}; {{Numbers 14:22|Numbers 14:22}}; {{Daniel 1:20|Daniel 1:20}}).

- Job believed justice delayed and that God was unfair it how he had treated him ({{Job 19:7|19:7}}; {{Job 19:8-12|19:8–12}}). Later, Elihu and God disagreed ({{Job 34:12|34:12}}; {{Job 40:2|40:2}}).

- *drawn His net around me*: Job might have been replying to Bildad’s accusation ({{Job 18:8-10|18:8–10}}).
*my own family*: Job might have meant his tribe, his parents, his children, or his siblings.
*escaped by the skin of my teeth*: This figure of speech means a narrow escape. In Hebrew, it might also suggest that Job became as thin as a skeleton with a skull full of *teeth*.
*the hand of God has struck me*: God allowed Satan to harm Job ({{Job 1:11|1:11}}; {{Job 2:5|2:5}}).
*persecute* (literally *pursue*): Job said that God followed him like a someone hunting or a warrior ({{Job 10:16|10:16}}; {{Job 16:13|16:13}}).

Job wanted his words *inscribed* (carved) on a monument, not in a *book*. He wanted a record of his innocence that would last in response to Bildad's claim that he would become forgotten ({{Job 18:17|18:17}}).

Job's faith in a *Redeemer* (one who saves) could only become fulfilled in Christ. This was also true for his wish for an advocate and a witness in heaven ({{Job 9:33|9:33}}; {{Job 16:19|16:19}}). The term *Redeemer* (Hebrew *go’el*) comes from both criminal and civil law. A person could redeem or take revenge because of the wrong shedding of blood or redeem lost property. This included buying back a slave or marrying the widow who inherited the property ({{Numbers 35:12-18|Numbers 35:12–18}}; {{Leviticus 25:25|Leviticus 25:25}}, {{Leviticus 25:47-49|47–49}}; {{Leviticus 27:11-13|27:11–13}}; {{Ruth 3:13|Ruth 3:13}}). 

The Old Testament recognized the Lord as *Redeemer* ({{Exodus 6:6|Exodus 6:6}}; {{Psalm 19:14|Psalms 19:14}}; {{Psalm 103:4|103:4}}; {{Proverbs 23:10-11|Proverbs 23:10–11}}; {{Isaiah 43:1|Isaiah 43:1}}; {{Isaiah 54:5|Isaiah 54:5}}). New Testament Christians know the *Redeemer* as the Lord Jesus Christ ({{Ephesians 1:7|Ephesians 1:7}}, {{Ephesians 1:14|14}}; {{Hebrews 9:12|Hebrews 9:12}}; {{1 Peter 1:18|1 Peter 1:18}}). Job wanted his *Redeemer* to declare his innocence (see {{Job 1:1|Job 1:1}} and corresponding study note).
Job believed God would prove him right, even if he died first.

*I will see Him for myself*: This thought is like the psalmist's in "when I awake" ({{Psalm 17:15|Psalm 17:15}}). For Job, this hope could only come true by seeing God at the end of time when his body transformed ({{Matthew 5:8|Matthew 5:8}}; {{1 Corinthians 13:12|1 Corinthians 13:12}}; {{1 John 3:2|1 John 3:2}}; {{Revelation 1:7|Revelation 1:7}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:43-53|1 Corinthians 15:43–53}}; {{Philippians 3:21|Philippians 3:21}}).

According to biblical principles against lying, Job warned his friends to fear God's judgment ({{Job 13:7-11|13:7–11}}; see {{Matthew 7:1-2|Matthew 7:1–2}}; {{James 4:11-12|James 4:11–12}}). They eventually encountered his judgment, but they also received mercy ({{Job 42:7-8|Job 42:7–8}}).
*he will perish forever, like his own dung*: Compare {{1 Kings 14:9-11|1 Kings 14:9–11}}; {{2 Kings 9:36-37|2 Kings 9:36–37}}; {{Psalm 83:10|Psalm 83:10}}; {{Jeremiah 8:1-2|Jeremiah 8:1–2}}.
Riches stolen do not provide benefits that last because they obtain them in a dishonest way ({{Job 20:18-21|20:18–21}}).

*venom of cobras … poison of cobras … vipers*: In the end, evil people harm only themselves, not others ({{Matthew 3:7|Matthew 3:7}}; {{Romans 3:13|Romans 3:13}}; {{Proverbs 23:29-35|Proverbs 23:29–35}}).
*The streams* of olive oil and *rivers flowing with honey and cream *represent great blessings ({{Exodus 5:19|Exodus 5:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:3|Deuteronomy 27:3}}; {{Joel 3:18|Joel 3:18}}).

Like the grave or death, evil people always focus on themselves and never find satisfaction ({{Proverbs 27:20|Proverbs 27:20}}; {{Proverbs 30:15-16|30:15–16}}; {{Ecclesiastes 5:19|Ecclesiastes 5:19}}; {{Isaiah 57:20-21|Isaiah 57:20–21}}; {{Habakkuk 2:5|Habakkuk 2:5}}).

Evil people cannot avoid trouble (see {{Isaiah 24:17-18|Isaiah 24:17–18}}; {{Jeremiah 15:2-3|Jeremiah 15:2–3}}; {{Amos 5:19|Amos 5:19}}; {{Amos 9:1-2|9:1–2}}). When they escape one threat, another confronts them.

*Terrors*: These are terrors of death. Although the specific words "of death" are not in the Hebrew text, they are understood because the description talks about an arrowhead that glistens with blood (literally *with gall*). This indicates a deadly hit on an important organ in the body ({{Job 6:4|6:4}}; {{Job 16:13|16:13}}; {{Psalm 7:12|Psalm 7:12}}). The image conveys the serious threat and intense fear that comes with being in mortal danger.

Images like *darkness* and *fire* often symbolize God's presence, especially his judgment ({{Deuteronomy 4:11|Deuteronomy 4:11}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:22-23|5:22–23}}; {{Hebrews 12:18|Hebrews 12:18}}; {{Exodus 9:23-24|Exodus 9:23–24}}; {{Exodus 10:21-29|10:21–29}}).

Job’s friends claimed they were delivering God’s message of *consolation *or comfort. But Job found no comfort in their words. He asked them to comfort him by giving him silent attention ({{Job 15:11|15:11}}; {{Job 16:2|16:2}}; {{Job 13:5|13:5}}).

- *When I think about what I am saying*: Job felt upset about his horrible task of complaining against God and talking about his terrors ({{Job 13:3|13:3}}, {{Job 13:15-16|15–16}}, {{Job 13:22|22}}; {{Job 23:1-5|23:1–5}}; {{Job 6:4|6:4}}; {{Job 27:20|27:20}}; {{Job 30:15|30:15}}).

- *my body trembles*: This reaction is similar to that of the prophets Habakkuk, Ezekiel, and Daniel ({{Habakkuk 1:5|Habakkuk 1:5}}; {{Habakkuk 3:16|3:16}}; {{Ezekiel 3:14|Ezekiel 3:14}}; {{Daniel 8:27|Daniel 8:27}}; {{Daniel 10:8-9|10:8–9}}).

Despite what Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar claimed, Job observed that evil people have children and grandchildren ({{Job 5:4|5:4}}); {{Job 18:19|18:19}}; {{Job 20:10|20:10}}). These should be rewards for righteous people ({{Proverbs 17:6|Proverbs 17:6}}). But Job felt they would not be his reward ({{Job 1:18-19|Job 1:18–19}}; see also {{Job 42:13-16|42:13–16}}).

*the lamp of the wicked put out*: Job disagreed with Bildad and the standard perspective of wisdom ({{Job 18:5-6|18:5–6}}, {{Job 18:18|18}}; {{Proverbs 13:9|Proverbs 13:9}}; {{Proverbs 20:20|20:20}}; {{Job 24:20|24:20}}; see God’s comments at {{Job 38:15|Job 38:15}}).

- *It is said*: Job was quoting and responding to his friends' arguments. 

- *God lays up one’s punishment for his children*: Eliphaz and Zophar said this, but Job believed God should punish the people who sin ({{Job 5:4|5:4}}; {{Job 20:10|20:10}}; see {{Ezekiel 18:19-20|Ezekiel 18:19–20}}).

- This question assumes the answer that no one can teach God a lesson ({{Isaiah 40:13-14|Isaiah 40:13–14}}; {{Isaiah 45:9|45:9}}; {{Romans 11:34|Romans 11:34}}; {{1 Corinthians 2:16|1 Corinthians 2:16}}).

- The phrase *those on high* might refer to good or bad angels (demons) ({{1 Corinthians 6:3|1 Corinthians 6:3}}; {{2 Peter 2:4|2 Peter 2:4}}; {{Jude 6|Jude 1:6}}; {{Revelation 20:1-3|Revelation 20:1–3}}). Or, more likely, it refers to powerful people on earth ({{Job 34:17-19|Job 34:17–19}}).
*his bones are rich with marrow*: People once believed bones were the source of health.
*in the bitterness of his soul*: Job often complained about how life seemed useless ({{Job 3:20|3:20}}; {{Job 7:11|7:11}}; {{Job 9:18|9:18}}; {{Job 10:1|10:1}}).
*where are the tents in which the wicked dwell*: Job was echoing the words of Bildad, Eliphaz and Zophar ({{Job 8:22|8:22}}; {{Job 15:34|15:34}}; {{Job 20:26|20:26}}).
*The clods of the valley are sweet to him*: Job considered death as a relief ({{Job 3:17-18|3:17–18}}).
They told lies about Job and God ({{Job 13:4|13:4}}; {{Job 42:7|42:7}}).
In this third round of speeches, Job's friends plainly accuse him of being evil and sharing the fate of those who do evil.

- Eliphaz did not understand that God would *delight* in Job’s right relationship with him, just as God does with every *righteous* person ({{Job 1:8|1:8}}; {{Job 2:3|2:3}}; {{1 Chronicles 29:17|1 Chronicles 29:17}}; {{Psalm 147:10-11|Psalms 147:10–11}}; {{Proverbs 11:1|Proverbs 11:1}}, {{Proverbs 11:20|20}}; {{Proverbs 12:22|12:22}}). God would also* benefit* from Job’s steady faith, which exposed the lie in Satan’s challenge ({{Job 1:9-12|Job 1:9–12}}; {{Job 2:4-6|2:4–6}}).

- Job firmly claimed that he was *blameless* ({{Job 23:10-12|23:10–12}}). God said the same thing ({{Job 1:1|1:1}}, {{Job 1:8|8}}; {{Job 2:3|2:3}}).

The law and prophets forbade taking clothing as *security* for loans ({{Exodus 22:26-27|Exodus 22:26–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:10-13|Deuteronomy 24:10–13}}; {{Ezekiel 18:7-8|Ezekiel 18:7–8}}; {{Amos 2:8|Amos 2:8}}). In contrast, Job gave clothing to poor people ({{Job 31:19-20|Job 31:19–20}}).

The Old Testament assigns Israel the duty of caring for *widows* and *the fatherless* ({{Deuteronomy 10:18|Deuteronomy 10:18}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:29|14:29}}). It often condemns neglecting them as the worst evil against society ({{Exodus 22:22-24|Exodus 22:22–24}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:19|Deuteronomy 27:19}}). Job agreed that neglecting them was wrong but claimed he was innocent ({{Job 24:3|Job 24:3}}, {{Job 24:21|21}}; {{Job 29:12-13|29:12–13}}; {{Job 31:16-18|31:16–18}}, {{Job 31:21|21}}).
*What does God know?*: Job did not claim that God cannot see, but others have (see {{Psalm 10:11|Psalms 10:11}}; {{Psalm 73:11|73:11}}; {{Psalm 94:7|94:7}}).
*so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked*: Eliphaz repeated Job’s words to him ({{Job 21:16|21:16b}}).

*The righteous see it and are glad*: Those in a right relationship with God will be *glad* to *see* justice done and wrong things made right (see also {{Psalm 58:10-11|Psalm 58:10–11}}; {{Revelation 19:1-4|Revelation 19:1–4}}). Eliphaz's perspective overlooked God's wish "that the wicked should turn from their ways and live" (see {{Ezekiel 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11}}).

- The term *instruction* (Hebrew *torah*, also meaning "law," {{Deuteronomy 17:11|Deuteronomy 17:11}}), used in Job only here, often refers to the "Pentateuch" (Genesis through Deuteronomy). 

- *Receive … lay up*: See {{Deuteronomy 4:1-2|Deuteronomy 4:1–2}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:6-9|6:6–9}}; {{Psalm 119:11|Psalm 119:11}}; {{Proverbs 2:1-9|Proverbs 2:1–9}}. Job had done this thing ({{Job 23:12|Job 23:12}}).

*return to the Almighty*: Bildad and Zophar had already made a wrong application of this principle of the Bible ({{Job 8:5-6|8:5–6}}; {{Job 11:13-14|11:13–14}}; {{Isaiah 55:6-7|Isaiah 55:6–7}}; {{Hosea 14:1-2|Hosea 14:1–2}}; {{Zechariah 1:3|Zechariah 1:3}}; {{Acts 26:20|Acts 26:20}}). Now Eliphaz also makes a wrong application of it.

*gold of Ophir: Ophir* was probably in southern Arabia (see {{1 Kings 9:28|1 Kings 9:28}}; {{1 Kings 22:48|22:48}}). The *gold of Ophir* set the standard for fine gold ({{Isaiah 13:12|Isaiah 13:12}}). Queens wore it at weddings ({{Psalm 45:9|Psalm 45:9}}).

God promises to be a "treasure" for his people ({{Psalm 16:5|Psalm 16:5}}; {{Isaiah 33:6|Isaiah 33:6}}; {{Matthew 19:21|Matthew 19:21}}; {{Mark 10:21|Mark 10:21}}). Even if they own nothing, they will be "rich" ({{2 Corinthians 6:10|2 Corinthians 6:10}}; {{James 2:5|James 2:5}}).

- Ironically, Job will pray, God will hear, and Eliphaz will benefit ({{Job 42:8|42:8}}).

- *you will fulfill your vows*: People often vowed after God forgave them ({{Hosea 14:2|Hosea 14:2}}; {{Jonah 1:16|Jonah 1:16}}; {{Jonah 2:9|2:9}}). They also vowed when asking help from God ({{Judges 11:29-40|Judges 11:29–40}}; {{1 Samuel 1:1-28|1 Samuel 1:1–28}}). *Vows* mean a serious commitments or to swear a promise ({{Numbers 30:2|Numbers 30:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 23:23|Deuteronomy 23:23}}; {{Psalm 22:25|Psalms 22:25}}; {{Psalm 61:5|61:5}}, {{Psalm 61:8|8}}; {{Psalm 116:14|116:14}}, {{Psalm 116:18|18}}; {{Ecclesiastes 5:4-5|Ecclesiastes 5:4–5}}).

This difficult text probably shows how effective the prayer of a person in a right relationship with God can be. The idea appears throughout the Bible ({{Psalm 34:15|Psalms 34:15}}, {{Psalm 34:17|17}}; {{Psalm 145:18|145:18}}; {{Proverbs 15:8|Proverbs 15:8}}, {{Job 15:29|29}}; {{James 5:16|James 5:16}}; see also {{Genesis 18:23-32|Genesis 18:23–32}}; {{Genesis 19:29|19:29}}; {{Genesis 20:7|20:7}}, {{Genesis 20:17|17}}; {{Genesis 32:28|32:28}}; {{Exodus 9:28-32|Exodus 9:28–32}}; {{Exodus 17:11|17:11}}; {{Exodus 32:10-14|32:10–14}}; {{Romans 5:19|Romans 5:19}}).
Job released his earlier doubts ({{Job 9:14-20|9:14–20}}, {{Job 9:32|32}}). Now he expresses confidence that he could present his *complaint* to God with success.

*plead my case*: Job wanted to present his legal *case* to God ({{Job 13:3|13:3}}, {{Job 13:18|18}}, {{Job 13:22|22}}; {{Job 16:21|16:21}}; {{Job 31:35|31:35}}). Abraham pleaded directly with God about Sodom ({{Genesis 18:25-32|Genesis 18:25–32}}). Moses did the same for Israel ({{Exodus 32:12-13|Exodus 32:12–13}}; {{Numbers 14:13-19|Numbers 14:13–19}}).

- Earlier, Job thought God was too powerful for him to "summon" ({{Job 9:19|9:19}}). He asked for "a mediator" and requested that God not "frighten" him ({{Job 9:33-34|9:33–34}}; {{Job 13:21|13:21}}). Here, he showed more hope that God would give him a fair legal hearing. 

- *delivered*: Job wanted God to declare him innocent, not forgive him as if he were guilty ({{Job 13:18|13:18}}; see {{Psalm 17:2-3|Psalms 17:2–3}}; {{Psalm 26:1-3|26:1–3}}).

*has tested *me: Job did not want the kind of punishment that would make him clean as through "a refiner’s fire" ({{Proverbs 17:3|Proverbs 17:3}}; {{Zechariah 13:9|Zechariah 13:9}}; {{Malachi 3:2-3|Malachi 3:2–3}}). He wanted a test to show he was already as pure *as gold* and did not need to change his life ({{Job 22:23|Job 22:23}}).

- *Terrified in His presence*: See {{Psalm 77:3|Psalms 77:3}}; {{Psalm 88:16|88:16}}; {{Psalm 119:120|119:120}}.

- Job had earlier complained about being in *darkness* ({{Job 19:8|Job 19:8}}). Eliphaz and Bildad said this fate is for the evil person ({{Job 15:22|15:22}}; {{Job 22:1|22:1}}; {{Job 18:6|18:6}}, {{Job 18:18|18}}).

*reserve times*: God sets times for *judgment* ({{Ecclesiastes 3:17|Ecclesiastes 3:17}}; {{Ecclesiastes 8:6|8:6}}; {{Daniel 2:21|Daniel 2:21}}; {{Luke 21:22-24|Luke 21:22–24}}). But we do not know when they are ({{Acts 1:7|Acts 1:7}}). He will reveal them at the right time ({{1 Thessalonians 5:1-28|1 Thessalonians 5:1–28}}; {{1 Timothy 6:15|1 Timothy 6:15}}).

The books of the law, wisdom literature, and prophecy all condemned moving markers of boundaries ({{Deuteronomy 19:14|Deuteronomy 19:14}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:17|27:17}}; {{Proverbs 22:28|Proverbs 22:28}}; {{Proverbs 23:10|23:10}}; see study note on Hosea 5:10).
This list of criminal behaviors first emphasizes crimes against weak people ({{Job 24:2-12|24:2–12}}). Then it examines the criminals themselves ({{Job 24:13-17|24:13–17}}).

The law prohibited taking essential possessions as security or a down payment for a loan ({{Job 22:6-9|22:6–9}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:6|Deuteronomy 24:6}}, {{Deuteronomy 24:10-13|10–13}}, {{Deuteronomy 24:17-21|17–21}}).

*glean the vineyards of the wicked*: Job described the desperate situation of poor people. If someone stole their fields like in the case of Naboth's vineyard, the poor person would harvest for the thieves instead of for themselves ({{Job 24:2|24:2}}; see {{1 Kings 21:1-29|1 Kings 21:1–29}}). They would only get the bits that remained. If the poor had to *glean* from *fields* of the *wicked* people, they would receive nothing ({{Leviticus 19:10|Leviticus 19:10}}; {{Leviticus 23:22|23:22}}). But if they would try to *gather *from the fields of just people, they would be something left for them ({{Leviticus 19:9-10|Leviticus 19:9–10}}; {{Leviticus 23:22|23:22}}; {{Ruth 2:1-23|Ruth 2:1–23}}).

Those who did not lend fairly sometimes took the clothing or blankets of those in debt as a security for the loan. This left those in debt without proper clothing or covering ({{Job 22:6|22:6}}; {{Exodus 22:26-27|Exodus 22:26–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:11-13|Deuteronomy 24:11–13}}; {{Amos 2:8|Amos 2:8}}).
*the nursing child of the poor is seized for a debt*: See {{2 Kings 4:1|2 Kings 4:1}}; {{Nehemiah 5:1-5|Nehemiah 5:1–5}}; {{Matthew 18:25|Matthew 18:25}}.

Forcing workers to *tread the winepresses* while they *go thirsty* violates the principle of letting workers enjoy some of the produce they are harvesting (see {{Deuteronomy 25:4|Deuteronomy 25:4}}; compare {{2 Timothy 2:6|2 Timothy 2:6}}).

*yet God charges no one with wrongdoing*: Job thought that, unlike God's usual character, God did not help those treated wrong or stop evil people from hurting their victims ({{Exodus 2:23-24|Exodus 2:23–24}}; {{Psalm 12:5|Psalm 12:5}}; {{Job 24:2-12|Job 24:2–12}}; {{Job 24:13-17|24:13–17}}).

These ideas seem to go against Job's observations. Some scholars think Bildad or Zophar might have said them. However, Job might have been speaking against evil people, making fun of his friends' opinions by quoting them. Or he might have meant that the fate of evil people also affects those in a right relationship with God. His friends described this earlier ({{Job 5:2-7|5:2–7}}; {{Job 15:17-25|15:17–25}}; {{Job 8:8-19|8:8–19}}; {{Job 18:5-21|18:5–21}}; {{Job 20:4-29|20:4–29}}; {{Job 21:23-26|21:23–26}}).

Eliphaz stated that being innocent or pure is almost impossible ({{Job 4:17-19|4:17–19}}; {{Job 15:14-16|15:14–16}}). A person can achieve it only after suffering ({{Job 22:21-23|22:21–23}}). Bildad argued that only those who are completely blameless can hope to be pure ({{Job 8:20|8:20}}).

Job’s friends did not help him ({{Job 12:2|12:2}}; {{Job 16:4|16:4}}). Bildad's claim that innocence was impossible upset Job deeply ({{Job 10:1-7|10:1–7}}; {{Job 13:3|13:3}}, {{Job 13:13-19|13–19}}; {{Job 16:18-21|16:18–21}}; {{Job 19:23-27|19:23–27}}; {{Job 23:2-7|23:2–7}}).

Eliphaz, Zophar, and Elihu all claimed that the right *spirit* was guiding them ({{Job 4:15|4:15}}; {{Job 20:3|20:3}}; {{Job 32:18|32:18}}; {{Job 33:4|33:4}}; see also {{Jeremiah 29:8-9|Jeremiah 29:8–9}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}}; {{1 John 4:1|1 John 4:1}}).

- The Hebrew word,* Sheol,* is where all dead people go. It is *beneath the waters*.

- The Hebrew word,* Abaddon,* is the place where evil people go to their destruction.

The Hebrew word *tsapon* means *north.* It sometimes refers to the northern mountain of the Canaanite gods, similar to Mount Olympus ({{Genesis 13:14|Genesis 13:14}}). The Berean Standard Bible refers to it as the sky, stretched *over empty space* (see {{Genesis 1:6-8|Genesis 1:6–8}}; {{Psalm 104:2-3|Psalm 104:2–3}}; {{Isaiah 40:22-23|Isaiah 40:22–23}}).

People once believed that mountains at the edge of the horizon were the *foundations* or "pillars" of heaven or the earth ({{Judges 16:25-26|Judges 16:25–26;}} {{Job 9:6|Job 9:6}}). They thought these mountains extended from beneath the sea's waters up to the clouds, supporting the dome of the heavens ({{Jonah 2:6|Jonah 2:6}}).

- *He stirred the sea* (compare {{Exodus 14:21|Exodus 14:21}}; {{Mark 4:39|Mark 4:39}}; compare {{Isaiah 51:15|Isaiah 51:15}}; {{Jeremiah 31:35|Jeremiah 31:35}}). God performed a miracle for his people. 

- *He shattered Rahab*: God showed control over the sea symbolized as a monster ("Rahab"), challenging myths about the sea being divine. See also {{Psalm 74:13-14|Psalms 74:13–14}}; {{Psalm 89:9-10|89:9–10}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}; {{Isaiah 51:9-10|51:9–10}}.

- *His breath* (or *wind*): God's authority clears *the skies* after a storm ({{Job 26:12|26:12}}). 

- *The fleeing serpent* relates to "Yam" and "Rahab" (see study note on 7:12). It provides background for the image of Satan as a "dragon" ({{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}; also {{Psalm 74:13-14|Psalm 74:13–14}}; see {{Genesis 3:15|Genesis 3:15}}; {{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}; {{Revelation 12:9|Revelation 12:9}}; {{Revelation 20:2|20:2}}).
*Job continued his discourse*: He no longer responded to his three friends. Instead, he returned to the themes of his opening statement ({{Job 3:1-26|3:1–26}}).

- The Bible allows for making a vow to the living God ({{Ruth 3:13|Ruth 3:13}}; {{1 Samuel 20:21|1 Samuel 20:21}}; {{1 Samuel 25:26|25:26}}; {{1 Kings 17:1|1 Kings 17:1}}; {{1 Kings 18:15|18:15}}; {{Jeremiah 4:2|Jeremiah 4:2}}). But sometimes people make silly or false vows ({{1 Samuel 14:39|1 Samuel 14:39}}, {{1 Samuel 14:45|45}}; {{Jeremiah 5:2|Jeremiah 5:2}}). 

- Elihu later criticized Job for claiming that God *deprived me of justice* ({{Job 34:5|Job 34:5}}).

- *embittered my soul* ({{Job 7:11|7:11}}; {{Job 10:1|10:1}}; {{Job 21:25|21:25}}): Compare Naomi and the widow from Shunem after losing her son ({{Ruth 1:20-21|Ruth 1:20–21}}; {{2 Kings 4:27|2 Kings 4:27}}).

Job found it wrong and offensive to admit that his friends were correct. It was a terrible act to condemn an innocent man like him ({{Exodus 23:7|Exodus 23:7}}; {{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}; {{Proverbs 17:15|17:15}}).
Some interpreters think this is a new speech by Zophar. Without it, Zophar has no speech in this cycle.

This section is an isolated speech. There is no speaker listed, so it might continue from earlier words. Some see it as a creative summary by the author of Job. It emphasizes the limits of human wisdom and sets the stage for the Lord's speeches.
People who mined would melt rock by burning a *fire* in a mine for days or weeks to extract the solid matter (ore). Some used *fire* and then cold water to crack the rocks.
Wisdom does not come from people. God is the true source of wisdom ({{Job 28:23-28|28:23–28}}).
The metals, gems, and glass listed here were valuable in the ancient world. However, the speaker says wisdom is more valuable than wealth.

When God looks across the entire earth, he sees his wisdom in his creation ({{Job 28:23|28:23}}). God later showed his wisdom to Job by taking him on a tour of the universe (chapters {{Job 38:1-41:34|38–41}}).
