*the fear of the Lord *(Hebrew, *’adonay*): In the book of Job, this name for God appears only here. This might suggest that chapter {{Job 28:1-28|28}} is a poem by the person narrating.

Job compares his past happiness, honor, and wealth with his current loss of social dignity and divine friendship (chapters {{Job 29:1-25|29}}and {{Job 30:1-31|30}}). He ends his speech with broad vows of innocence (chapter {{Job 31:1-40|31}}).

In other parts of the text, Job uses the Hebrew word *shamar* to describe what he sees as God's severe surveillance ({{Job 10:14|10:14}}; {{Job 13:27|13:27}}; {{Job 14:16|14:16}}). However, here it refers to God's kind care, meaning *watched over* ({{Psalm 121:3-8|Psalm 121:3–8}}).
*The city gate *served as the town's administrative center (see {{Ruth 4:1-2|Ruth 4:1–2}}, {{Ruth 4:11|11}}).

Job described his *righteousness* using royal imagery. In the Bible, a *robe* often symbolizes *righteousness* ({{Psalm 132:9|Psalm 132:9}}; {{Isaiah 59:17|Isaiah 59:17}}; {{Isaiah 61:10|Isaiah 61:10}}; {{Romans 13:14|Romans 13:14}}; {{Revelation 19:8|Revelation 19:8}}).
Job was active in searching out and helping strangers in need.

*and multiply my days as the sand* (literally *after I have counted my days like sand*): Job believed the length of his years showed God's blessing. This was similar to the numerous people descended from Abraham or the abundance of supplies Joseph had in Egypt ({{Genesis 15:5|Genesis 15:5}}; {{Genesis 32:12|32:12}}; {{Genesis 41:49|Genesis 41:49}}).

In the past, Job was a *comforter of the mourners* ({{Job 4:3-4|4:3–4}}). This verse is a prophetic command closely linked to the work of the Christ ({{Isaiah 40:1|Isaiah 40:1}}; {{Isaiah 61:1-3|61:1–3}}; {{Luke 4:18-19|Luke 4:18–19}}; see also {{2 Corinthians 1:3-4|2 Corinthians 1:3–4}}).

In the past, the most important members of society praised Job ({{Job 29:11|29:11}}). Now, the least important made fun of him and spit in his face ({{Job 30:1|30:1,}}{{Job 30:10|10}}). Compare with {{Psalm 35:15|Psalms 35:15}}; {{Psalm 69:12|69:12}}; {{Mark 14:65|Mark 14:65}}; {{Mark 15:17-20|15:17–20}}.

They live in scary valleys (*wadis*), caves (*holes*), and among *rocks*. 

The miserable life of those making fun of Job was like: 

- Israel’s situation under Midianite abuse ({{Judges 6:2|Judges 6:2}}).

- David’s life when he fled from King Saul ({{1 Samuel 22:1-2|1 Samuel 22:1–2}}).

- The prophet Elijah’s life as he waited for the Lord’s instruction ({{1 Kings 17:3-8|1 Kings 17:3–8}}).
*they mock me*: See also {{Job 17:6|17:6}}; compare with {{Psalm 69:12|Psalm 69:12}}; {{Lamentations 3:14|Lamentations 3:14}}, {{Lamentations 3:63|63}}.

- *keep far from me*: See also {{Job 19:13-15|19:13–15}}; compare {{Psalm 88:8|Psalm 88:8}}; {{Proverbs 19:7|Proverbs 19:7}}; {{Matthew 26:56|Matthew 26:56}}.

- Spitting in someone's face showed extreme dislike or hatred ({{Deuteronomy 25:9|Deuteronomy 25:9}}; {{Isaiah 50:6|Isaiah 50:6}}; {{Matthew 26:67|Matthew 26:67}}; {{Matthew 27:30|27:30}}; {{Mark 14:65|Mark 14:65}}).

- The series of images here shows a military attack on a city with strong defenses. Job had already used this image to describe God's attack on him ({{Job 19:10-12|Job 19:10–12}}).

- The word translated as *snares* might refer to ramps raised against a city's walls. A siege ramp was a large sloped structure of earth and stones that armies built against city walls. These ramps allowed attacking soldiers to climb up to the top of the walls during a battle.
*He seizes me by the collar*: The Hebrew in this verse is hard to translate. It might mean Job feels like God is choking him and he is a throw him into the mud (compare {{Job 30:19|30:19}}).
*dust and ashes*: Earlier, Job sat among the *ashes* in pain ({{Job 2:8|2:8}}). Later, he would sit in *dust and ashes* to "repent" ({{Job 42:6|42:6}}).
*You do not answer*: Job often complained about this ({{Job 9:16|9:16}}; {{Job 19:7|19:7}}; {{Job 23:2-9|23:2–9}}; {{Job 31:35|31:35}}). But God soon responded ({{Job 38:1|38:1}}).

Job felt like he was caught in a storm and blown around like useless "straw" or "chaff" ({{Job 9:17|9:17}}; {{Job 21:18|21:18}}; {{Job 27:21|27:21}}; {{Psalm 1:4|Psalm 1:4}}; {{Isaiah 17:13|Isaiah 17:13}}).
Before his testing began, people respected Job in the public square ({{Job 29:7-10|29:7–10}}, {{Job 29:21-25|21–25}}). He helped those in need ({{Job 29:11-17|29:11–17}}).

Job might have been expressing how he saw himself, how others saw him, or both. By saying he was *a brother of jackals, a companion to owls,* Job might have been describing his deep grief ({{Micah 1:8|Micah 1:8}}). People associated *jackals* with things devastated or ruins (see {{Psalm 63:10|Psalm 63:10}}; {{Isaiah 13:22|Isaiah 13:22}}; {{Isaiah 34:13|34:13}}; {{Isaiah 35:7|35:7}}; {{Jeremiah 9:11|Jeremiah 9:11}}; {{Jeremiah 10:22|10:22}}; {{Jeremiah 49:33|49:33}}; {{Jeremiah 51:37|51:37}}; {{Lamentations 5:18|Lamentations 5:18}}; {{Ezekiel 13:4|Ezekiel 13:4}}; {{Malachi 1:3|Malachi 1:3}}).
People with a comfortable life had skin protected from the sun and wind. Dark skin suggested physical and social decline ({{Lamentations 4:8|Lamentations 4:8}}; {{Lamentations 5:10|5:10}}).

- Job made a promise with himself about his eyes, including an oath against himself (curse) (see {{Matthew 5:28-29|Matthew 5:28–29}}). Job might have focused on wrong desire because the eyes are often the first to commit sin ({{Genesis 3:6|Genesis 3:6}}). 

- Looking with wrong desire at *a virgin* violates the spirit of the seventh commandment ({{Deuteronomy 5:18|Deuteronomy 5:18}}, see {{Matthew 5:27-28|Matthew 5:27–28}}). It could violate the tenth commandment as well ({{Deuteronomy 5:21|Deuteronomy 5:21}}).

Job called down wrong against himself (curses) if he was guilty of the accusations against him. Apart from mentioning idolatry (worship of false gods), Job spoke about how loyal he was to God by focusing on the second half of the Ten Commandments ({{Job 31:26-27|31:26–27}}). The summary of these is: “love your neighbor as yourself” ({{Leviticus 19:18|Leviticus 19:18}}; {{Romans 13:9|Romans 13:9}}).

- If Job had lied in a business deal, it would violate the eighth commandment ({{Deuteronomy 5:19|Deuteronomy 5:19}}). If he lied in court, it would violate the ninth commandment ({{Deuteronomy 5:20|Deuteronomy 5:20}}). This sin would deserve judgment of fire ({{Revelation 21:8|Revelation 21:8}}).

- If Job desired his neighbor's possessions, he would violate the tenth commandment ({{Deuteronomy 5:21|Deuteronomy 5:21}}).

- *then may another eat*: This was also speaking against himself (a curse).

- Whether she tempted him or he waited for her, if Job desired his neighbor’s wife, he would violate the seventh and tenth commandments ({{Job 24:15-16|24:15–16}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:18|Deuteronomy 5:18}}, {{Matthew 5:27-28|Matthew 5:27–28}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:21|Deuteronomy 5:21}}).

- *grind for*: This might refer to servitude or sexual relations ({{Exodus 11:5|Exodus 11:5}}).

The Hebrew term *zimmah* is associated with sexual crimes like incest (“it is depraved,” {{Leviticus 18:17|Leviticus 18:17}}), gang-rape (“a lewd and disgraceful act,” {{Judges 20:6|Judges 20:6}}), and prostitution ("indecency," {{Ezekiel 23:49|Ezekiel 23:49}}).
The Old Testament rarely links *fire* with hell (*Abaddon*) or the grave (see {{Deuteronomy 32:22|Deuteronomy 32:22}}).

- *Rejected … manservant or maidservant*: This might refer to violating the fourth commandment ({{Deuteronomy 5:12-15|Deuteronomy 5:12–15}}).

- *He who made me in the womb also make them*: Job applied the idea of being made in God's image to the poor person and even to slaves ({{Proverbs 14:31|Proverbs 14:31}}; {{Proverbs 22:2|22:2}}).
*I had support in the gate*: Job had respect and they regarded him as part of the high class ({{Job 29:7-10|29:7–10}}).

If someone used an arm for a sinful action, having it* torn from its socket *would be a fitting punishment ({{Job 31:21|31:21}}). This would be better than encountering God's judgment (compare {{Matthew 5:28-30|Matthew 5:28–30}}).

*If I have put my trust in gold*: Job did not state the result of this vow because the "if-then" pattern was now obvious ({{Job 31:5-23|31:5–23}}). He rejected the judgment Eliphaz implied ({{Job 22:24-25|22:24–25}}; see {{Psalm 52:7|Psalms 52:7}}; {{Psalm 62:10|62:10}}; {{1 Timothy 6:10|1 Timothy 6:10}}, {{1 Timothy 6:17|17}}).
*rejoiced in my great wealth*: See {{Deuteronomy 8:17-18|Deuteronomy 8:17–18}}; compare {{Isaiah 10:12-14|Isaiah 10:12–14}}; {{Daniel 4:28-30|Daniel 4:28–30}}; {{Hosea 12:8|Hosea 12:8}}.

*if I have beheld the sun … or the moon*: This vow denies violating the first commandment (compare {{Jeremiah 8:2|Jeremiah 8:2}}; {{Jeremiah 44:17|44:17}}; {{Ezekiel 8:16|Ezekiel 8:16}}; {{Acts 7:43|Acts 7:43}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:7|Deuteronomy 5:7}}; see {{Deuteronomy 4:19|Deuteronomy 4:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:2-7|17:2–7}}).

The sins of adultery and worshiping the sun and moon had the death penalty (compare {{Job 31:1|31:1}}, {{Job 31:9-12|9–12}}). Both were sins that tempted the inner being of a person through the eyes. Judges tried both types of sin in court.

- *My heart was secretly enticed*: See {{Job 31:9|31:9}}. 

- *threw a kiss from my mouth*: Compare {{1 Kings 19:18|1 Kings 19:18}}; {{Hosea 13:2|Hosea 13:2}}.

- In Israel, the role of judges was to punish those worshiping idols (false gods) by execution (see {{Job 31:11|31:11}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:2-7|Deuteronomy 17:2–7}}). 

- Denying *God on high *violated the first commandment ({{Deuteronomy 5:7|Deuteronomy 5:7}}).

- *I have rejoiced in my enemy’s ruin*: See {{Proverbs 24:17-18|Proverbs 24:17–18}}; compare {{2 Samuel 16:5-8|2 Samuel 16:5–8}}.

- Speaking evil against (*a curse*) anyone went against the spirit of the sixth commandment ({{Deuteronomy 5:17|Deuteronomy 5:17}}; see {{Matthew 5:21-22|Matthew 5:21–22}}).

- It was against God's will to seek revenge ({{Matthew 5:43-44|Matthew 5:43–44}}; {{Romans 12:14|Romans 12:14}}; {{James 3:6-10|James 3:6–10}}; {{1 Peter 3:9|1 Peter 3:9}}).

*no stranger had to lodge on the street*: The Old Testament values hosting strangers (hospitality) ({{Genesis 18:1-13|Genesis 18:1–13}}; {{Genesis 19:2-3|19:2–3}}; {{Judges 19:20-21|Judges 19:20–21}}). The New Testament commands it ({{Matthew 25:35|Matthew 25:35}}; {{Romans 12:13|Romans 12:13}}; {{1 Timothy 3:2|1 Timothy 3:2}}; {{Hebrews 13:2|Hebrews 13:2}}; {{1 Peter 4:9|1 Peter 4:9}}).
*Here is my signature*: Job wanted to make the events official ({{Job 19:23-24|19:23–24}}).
*carry it on my shoulder* (compare {{Exodus 28:12|Exodus 28:12}}; {{Isaiah 22:22|Isaiah 22:22}}): He would take full responsibility for his actions.
When someone made a wrong accusation against a prince, he could appeal to his king.
The *land* was the main "witness" to the crimes done on it ({{Job 20:27|20:27}}; see {{Genesis 4:10|Genesis 4:10}}; compare {{James 5:4|James 5:4}}).

*let briers grow*: Job cursed himself (spoke evil against himself), echoing when God first "cursed" Adam ({{Genesis 3:17-18|Genesis 3:17–18}}; see also {{Isaiah 7:25|Isaiah 7:25}}; {{Zephaniah 2:9|Zephaniah 2:9}}).
Job's three friends did not succeed in comforting him (see {{Job 2:11|2:11}}; {{Job 6:14-30|6:14–30}}; {{Job 13:4|13:4}}; {{Job 16:2|16:2}}; {{Job 19:21|19:21}}; {{Job 42:10|42:10}}).

Elihu was younger than Job’s other friends. It’s thought that he was also from Edom. Elihu was angry at Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. They hadn’t fully answered Job or shown how Job was wrong.

Elihu thought that it was wrong for Job to question God. He thought that Job believed he was right and that God was wrong. This made Elihu angry. But the answer he gave about Job’s suffering was like the answers of the others. Elihu believed that God allowed Job to suffer in order to correct him. The suffering was seen as a warning to keep Job from sinning. Elihu thought that this would save Job from being put to death for his sins.

Elihu understood that God never does anything evil, wrong or unfair. So he thought it was wrong for Job to think that God treated him unfairly. He thought that this showed that Job was full of pride. Elihu understood that God has complete power over everything. God is the Creator who made the world and everything in it. God is the only one able to keep the life of the world going. For Elihu, this meant that people can’t understand God’s reasons for doing something. So he thought that people shouldn’t ask questions about God’s reasons.
After three rounds of speeches between Job and his friends, a new voice speaks. Elihu, a young man, has listened to everything the others said.

- *The Buzite*: Buz had ties with Aram and Arabia, similar to Uz ({{Genesis 22:21|Genesis 22:21}}; {{Jeremiah 25:23|Jeremiah 25:23}}; {{Job 1:1|Job 1:1}}).

- *Elihu* often said he was angry. He probably considered his anger as righteous "zeal" ({{Psalm 69:9|Psalm 69:9}}).

*Elihu* respected elders, following a common principle (see also {{Job 12:12|12:12}}; {{Job 15:10|15:10}}; {{Leviticus 19:32|Leviticus 19:32}}; {{1 Timothy 5:1|1 Timothy 5:1}}; {{1 Peter 5:5|1 Peter 5:5}}).

The *spirit in a man* might not be God's Spirit of prophecy that Elihu later mentions, as Eliphaz had done ({{Job 33:14-15|33:14–15}}; {{Job 4:12-17|4:12–17}}; compare {{Job 32:18-20|32:18–20}}). This *spirit* might simply exist because of creation ({{Job 33:4|33:4}}; {{Genesis 2:7|Genesis 2:7}}; {{Acts 17:25|Acts 17:25}}).

Some translations read, "*you are silent, now that you stand and no longer reply.*" Thus, Elihu addresses Job's friends. The Berean Standard Bible translates *they are silent, now that they stand and no longer reply.* This interprets Elihu talking to Job about his friends.

- The length of Elihu’s speech shows he had many words to share ({{Job 32:1-37:24|32:1–37:24}}).

- Elihu probably believed the *spirit* (Hebrew *ruakh*) *within* him urged him to speak ({{Job 32:8|32:8}}, {{Job 32:19-20|19–20}}; {{Psalm 39:3|Psalm 39:3}}). But the reader might regard him as just full of *wind* (an alternate meaning of the Hebrew *ruakh*; see study note on Job 15:2–3).

- Like Zophar, Elihu needed to speak to *find relief* (compare {{Job 20:2|20:2}}).
*hear*: Elihu asked the others to *hear *him, just as Job had also requested ({{Job 33:1|33:1}}; {{Job 34:2|34:2}}, {{Job 34:16|16}}; {{Job 13:6|13:6}}).
Elihu invited Job to present his *case*, acting as if he were God or the judge Job had been seeking ({{Job 9:32-35|9:32–35}}).

- *no fear of me should terrify you*: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar had tried to use God's terrors to scare Job ({{Job 15:21|15:21}}, {{Job 15:24|24}}; {{Job 22:10|22:10}}; {{Job 18:11|18:11}}, {{Job 18:14|14}}; {{Job 20:25|20:25}}; {{Job 6:4|6:4}}; {{Job 7:14|7:14}}; {{Job 9:34|9:34}}; {{Job 13:21|13:21}}; {{Job 23:15|23:15}}).

- Elihu promised not to be harsh with Job, but he later violated his promise ({{Job 34:7-9|34:7–9}}, {{Job 34:33-37|33–37}}).

Job often complained about God's constant surveillance ({{Job 7:20|7:20}}; {{Job 10:14|10:14}}; {{Job 13:27|13:27}}). He wanted relief from having every move examined ({{Job 14:16|14:16}}; {{Job 29:2|29:2}}).
Job's main complaint was that God did not answer him ({{Job 9:16|9:16}}; {{Job 19:7|19:7}}; {{Job 23:2-7|23:2–7}}).
*from perishing by the sword*: This phrase can also mean "from crossing over the river of death" (New Living Translation). Both translations make sense in the context (compare {{Job 36:12|36:12}}).
*messengers of death*: Compare: {{Exodus 12:23|Exodus 12:23}}; {{2 Samuel 24:16|2 Samuel 24:16}}; {{1 Corinthians 10:10|1 Corinthians 10:10}}.
An angel or messenger from heaven would act as the *mediator* Job desired (see {{Job 5:1|5:1}}; {{Job 9:33-34|9:33–34}}; {{Job 16:18-21|16:18–21}}).
The ultimate *ransom* is Christ ({{Matthew 20:28|Matthew 20:28}}; {{Romans 3:24-25|Romans 3:24–25}}; {{1 Timothy 2:6|1 Timothy 2:6}}; {{1 Peter 1:18-19|1 Peter 1:18–19}}).
*he sees God’s face and shouts for joy*: Compare {{Numbers 6:24-26|Numbers 6:24–26}}; {{Psalm 67:1|Psalm 67:1}}; {{Acts 2:28|Acts 2:28}}; {{Jude 24|Jude 1:24}}.
It sounds ironic that Elihu says he *would like to vindicate* Job. He joined the discussion because Job would not admit he had sinned ({{Job 32:1-5|32:1–5}}).

*ear tests … mouth tastes*: Elihu repeated Job’s earlier complaint about the other counselors’ weak argument that, "Wisdom is found with the elderly" ({{Job 12:11-12|12:11–12}}; see {{Job 6:30|6:30}}; {{Hebrews 5:14|Hebrews 5:14}}).

- Eliphaz accused Job of lying ({{Job 15:5|15:5}}). This was something Job feared would happen ({{Job 6:28-29|6:28–29}}).

- *My wound* (literally *My arrow*): For the connection with the Lord’s "arrows," see {{Job 6:4|6:4}}; {{Job 16:13|16:13}}; {{Jeremiah 10:19|Jeremiah 10:19}}; {{Jeremiah 15:18|15:18}}; {{Jeremiah 30:12|30:12}}, {{Jeremiah 30:15|15}}; {{Lamentations 3:12|Lamentations 3:12}}; {{Micah 1:9|Micah 1:9}}; {{Nahum 3:19|Nahum 3:19}}.

Elihu later repeated this accusation ({{Job 35:3|35:3}}; compare {{Psalm 73:13|Psalm 73:13}}; {{Zephaniah 1:12|Zephaniah 1:12}}; {{Malachi 3:14|Malachi 3:14}}). But he misrepresented Job’s words ({{Job 9:22-23|Job 9:22–23}}; {{Job 21:15|21:15}}). Job had actually criticized those who had this perspective ({{Job 21:14-16|21:14–16}}).

The passage connects three ideas to the belief that God can do no wrong ({{Job 34:10|34:10}}, {{Job 34:12|12}}): 

- God rewards or punishes people based on their actions ({{Job 34:11|34:11}}); 

- As the creator, God does not have to answer to anyone ({{Job 34:13|34:13}}). 

- Every living being relies on God for life. God can take life away without being wrong ({{Job 34:14-15|34:14–15}}; compare {{Romans 9:19-29|Romans 9:19–29}}).

*according to a man’s deeds*: Compare {{Psalm 62:12|Psalm 62:12}}; {{Proverbs 24:12|Proverbs 24:12}}; {{Jeremiah 32:19|Jeremiah 32:19}}; {{Ezekiel 33:20|Ezekiel 33:20}}; {{Matthew 16:27|Matthew 16:27}}; {{Romans 2:6|Romans 2:6}}; {{Galatians 6:7-8|Galatians 6:7–8}}; {{1 Peter 1:17|1 Peter 1:17}}. The final judgment will occur at the end of time ({{2 Corinthians 5:10|2 Corinthians 5:10}}; {{Revelation 2:23|Revelation 2:23}}; {{Revelation 22:12|22:12}}).

- The implication was that God could not rule if he hated justice (see {{Romans 3:4-7|Romans 3:4–7}}; {{Romans 7:7|7:7}}, {{Romans 7:13|13}}; {{Romans 9:14|9:14}}; {{Galatians 2:17|Galatians 2:17}}; {{Galatians 6:14|6:14}}).

- Later, God also asked if Job intended to condemn the *mighty* judge ({{Job 40:8|Job 40:8}}).

*who is not partial to princes*: God's justice is not partial ({{Acts 10:34|Acts 10:34}}; {{Romans 2:11|Romans 2:11}}; {{Galatians 2:6|Galatians 2:6}}; {{Ephesians 6:9|Ephesians 6:9}}; {{Colossians 3:25|Colossians 3:25}}; {{1 Peter 1:17|1 Peter 1:17}}).

Evil people may try to hide in darkness ({{Jeremiah 23:24|Jeremiah 23:24}}). But they will not succeed ({{Psalm 139:11-12|Psalm 139:11–12}}; compare {{Amos 9:2-3|Amos 9:2–3}}). God reveals everything ({{1 Corinthians 4:5|1 Corinthians 4:5}}).

*God need not examine a man further*: Elihu said this to disagree with Job's wish for God to quickly announce a time of judgment ({{Job 21:19|21:19}}; {{Job 24:1|24:1}}). Elihu believed that God already understood all people perfectly without needing to set up a special court or investigation.

- God knows everything without needing to ask anyone ({{Job 34:25|34:25}}).

- *sets up others in their place*: {{Daniel 2:21|Daniel 2:21}}; {{Daniel 5:28-30|5:28–30}}.

When God shows justice openly, it causes evil people to have proper fear ({{Deuteronomy 21:21|Deuteronomy 21:21}}; {{1 Timothy 5:20|1 Timothy 5:20}}). This leads to public joy among people in a right relationship with God (compare {{Exodus 14:30-31|Exodus 14:30–31}}).
*Suppose someone says*: Elihu posed the indirect question, "Job, why won't you admit it?"
*tried to the utmost*: Zophar also said that Job should have suffered worse punishment than he did ({{Job 11:6|11:6}}).

Elihu tried to answer his own question ({{Job 35:2|35:2}}). 

But his response did not add anything new compared to:

- Zophar ({{Job 11:8-9|11:8–9}}).

- Eliphaz ({{Job 22:12|22:12}}).

- Bildad ({{Job 25:5-6|25:5–6}}).

- Job ({{Job 9:8-10|9:8–10}}). 

Elihu did not realize that all sin offends God ({{Genesis 39:9|Genesis 39:9}}; {{Matthew 25:41-46|Matthew 25:41–46}}; compare {{Proverbs 19:17|Proverbs 19:17}}).
Elihu echoed Job's words but then disagreed with them ({{Job 9:24|9:24}}; {{Job 12:6-10|12:6–10}}; {{Job 21:7-15|21:7–15}}, {{Job 21:17|17}}).
Elihu echoed his earlier accusation ({{Job 34:35|34:35}}). Later, God would agree ({{Job 38:2|38:2}}).
*one who is perfect in knowledge is with you*: Elihu probably was claiming to be sincere or that his logic had no flaw.

The Bible teaches that God always watches over *the righteous* ({{2 Chronicles 16:9|2 Chronicles 16:9}}; {{Psalm 33:18|Psalms 33:18}}; {{Psalm 34:15|34:15}}; {{1 Peter 3:12|1 Peter 3:12}}). This idea addresses Job's frustration about God's surveillance ({{Job 7:17-21|Job 7:17–21}}).

*If they obey and serve Him, then they end their days in prosperity*: This is a true biblical principle of dedication to God (repentance) (see {{Job 11:13-19|11:13–19}}; {{Job 22:21-25|22:21–25}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:30|Deuteronomy 4:30}}; {{Jeremiah 7:23|Jeremiah 7:23}}; {{Jeremiah 26:13|26:13}}).

The Hebrew *yadin* typically means *he judges* or *he governs.* But some commentators propose an alternate reading, *yazun* (meaning "he nourishes"). This aligns with the theme of God's provision ({{Job 38:26|Job 38:26}}; {{Psalm 65:9-13|Psalms 65:9–13}}; {{Psalm 104:13-15|104:13–15}}, {{Psalm 104:27-28|27–28}}). The more common meaning of *yadin* is “judge,” which would mean that God does all things to bless his people and judge his enemies ({{Job 37:11-13|Job 37:11–13}}; {{Job 38:22-23|38:22–23}}; see {{Genesis 6:17|Genesis 6:17}}; {{Genesis 19:24|19:24}}; {{Exodus 9:23-25|Exodus 9:23–25}}; {{Joshua 10:11-14|Joshua 10:11–14}}; {{1 Samuel 12:18|1 Samuel 12:18}}).

The Old Testament often links *thunder* to God's *voice* ({{Job 36:29|36:29}}, {{Job 36:33|33}}; {{Job 37:5|37:5}}; {{Job 38:1|38:1}}; {{Exodus 19:16-19|Exodus 19:16–19}}; {{Psalm 104:7|Psalm 104:7}}).
*He seals up the hand of every man … know His work*: The end of the farming season gives people time to think about God's control over everything.

God's actions can have multiple purposes. For example, storms can both destroy enemies and bring victory to God's people ({{Joshua 10:1-43|Joshua 10}}; {{Judges 4:1-24|Judges 4}}; {{1 Samuel 7:10-11|1 Samuel 7:10–11}}; {{Psalm 18:7-15|Psalms 18:7–15}}; {{Psalm 105:32-33|105:32–33}}).
The *hot south wind* made it very hot and uncomfortable.
*Should He be told that I want to speak? Would a man ask to be swallowed up?*: Contesting God's judgment might lead to severe punishment, even death (see {{Job 13:14|13:14}}).

*Out of the north* (Hebrew *from Zaphon*): In the literature of the ancient city of Ugarit, *Zaphon* was the northern mountain home of the false god "Baal." Here, it symbolically refers to the height of God's home in the heavens (see {{Isaiah 14:13-14|Isaiah 14:13–14}}).

- *The Almighty is beyond our reach*: Compare {{Job 11:7|11:7}}; {{Job 26:14|26:14}}; {{Romans 11:33|Romans 11:33}}; {{1 Timothy 6:16|1 Timothy 6:16}}.

- *His justice and great righteousness*: Compare {{Job 9:4|Job 9:4}}, {{Job 9:19|19}}; {{Job 12:13|12:13}}; {{Psalm 62:11|Psalms 62:11}}; {{Psalm 66:3|66:3}}; {{Psalm 93:1|93:1}}; {{Psalm 99:4|99:4}}.

*the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind*: The Old Testament often links storms with God's presence ({{2 Kings 2:1|2 Kings 2:1}}, {{2 Kings 2:11|11}}; {{Ezekiel 1:4|Ezekiel 1:4}}; {{Nahum 1:3|Nahum 1:3}}). Job finally had the chance to speak with God ({{Job 13:22-23|Job 13:22–23}}).

Job thought that God wouldn’t listen to him. Earlier Job had said he thought that God would send a storm to crush him. Job thought God would do this if he called out to God. Instead, God listened very closely.

God listened to everything that Job, Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar and Elihu said. Instead of crushing Job with a storm, God spoke to Job from a storm. God didn’t answer the questions Job had asked. He didn’t explain to Job why people suffer. God didn’t explain that Satan had suggested a test for Job. Instead, God asked Job many questions. God asked what things Job was able to do. Then God explained many of the things that he can do.

God created everything in heaven and on the earth. He makes sure that what he created works the way he wants it to. This includes the land, the water, the sky, the stars and the animals. God takes care of all animals. This includes animals that aren’t livestock raised by human beings.

God talked a lot about the sky, the earth and the animals. The way he talked about them showed Job something important. Human beings are only one part of what God created. As a human being, Job couldn’t understand everything about God’s creation. Job couldn’t understand everything that was needed to take care of creation. Job couldn’t understand God’s plans. Job couldn’t understand the reasons why God did what he did. And Job couldn’t do God’s work better than God did it. Job’s first answer to God was to remain silent.

God challenges Job. Job admits he cannot judge the moral world. God shows Job's ignorance of the natural world's elements related to the realm of heaven, weather, animals, and birds ({{Job 38:4-21|38:4–21}}; {{Job 38:22-38|22–38}}; {{Job 38:39-39:30|39–39:30}}).
*Then the LORD answered Job*: In this last part, the LORD challenges Job's strong self-defense by showing his works. This reminds Job of God's supreme greatness.

*obscures My counsel*: God’s accusation is similar to a charge made by Eliphaz and Elihu ({{Job 15:2|15:2}}; {{Job 34:35|34:35}}; {{Job 35:16|35:16}}). Job eventually admitted his guilt ({{Job 42:3|42:3}}).
God describes *the morning stars *as if they are people, similar to the description of angels ({{Job 1:6|1:6}}; {{Job 2:1|2:1}}).
*set in place its bars and doors*: God describes the sea as a dangerous creature that is kept under control.
*stand out like the folds of a garment*: The rising sun highlights the colors, shapes, and textures of objects.
*you were already born*: Compare with {{Proverbs 8:25|Proverbs 8:25}}. This sarcasm is similar to Eliphaz's words in {{Job 15:7|Job 15:7}}.

God stores up *snow* and *hail*, like the deep seas and winds ({{Psalm 33:7|Psalms 33:7}}; {{Psalm 135:7|135:7}}; {{Jeremiah 10:13|Jeremiah 10:13}}; {{Jeremiah 51:16|51:16}}). God uses these elements as weapons through storms he sends on the *day of war and battle* ({{Job 36:32|Job 36:32}}; {{Isaiah 30:30|Isaiah 30:30}}; {{Ezekiel 13:11-13|Ezekiel 13:11–13}}; {{Revelation 16:21|Revelation 16:21}}; for example, {{Joshua 10:11|Joshua 10:11}}; {{Judges 5:20-21|Judges 5:20–21}}; {{1 Samuel 7:10|1 Samuel 7:10}}.

- *The east wind* blows from the *desert*, drying up crops and seas ({{Genesis 41:6|Genesis 41:6}}, {{Genesis 41:23|23}}, {{Genesis 41:27|27}}; {{Jeremiah 4:11|Jeremiah 4:11}}; {{Jonah 4:8|Jonah 4:8}}; {{Exodus 14:21|Exodus 14:21}}; {{Isaiah 11:15|Isaiah 11:15}}). It is not like the heavy *rain* that causes floods.

- Helpful *rain* quenches *a barren land* ({{Psalm 104:10-11|Psalms 104:10–11}}; {{Psalm 107:35|107:35}}; {{Isaiah 35:7|Isaiah 35:7}}; {{Isaiah 58:11|58:11}}). This contrasts with both hot winds and flooding rains ({{Job 38:24|Job 38:24,}}{{Job 38:25|25}}).

*heart … mind*: These words can also mean "ibis" and "rooster*."* The Egyptians believed the ibis bird knew about the Nile's flooding, the most important event in Egypt. Israel’s rabbis (religious teachers with authority) believed the rooster bird could predict rain or its distinctive sound (crowing) marked day and night. The question would then be *Who taught the ibis and the rooster?* See also {{Psalm 51:6|Psalm 51:6}}; {{Proverbs 2:6|Proverbs 2:6}}; {{James 1:5|James 1:5}}, {{James 1:17|17}}.

*the wild donkey … scorns the tumult of the cit*y: This is the first example in a series of animals that think little of other animals not their equal (compare {{Job 39:18|39:18}}, {{Job 39:22|22}}; {{Job 41:29|41:29}}). These images show how God *scorns* the opposition of a person like Job (see {{Psalm 2:4|Psalm 2:4}}).

*The wild ox *now no longer exists and was already rare by the time of Moses. It was the strongest land animal in early Canaan. They never tamed this Old Testament symbol of strength ({{Numbers 23:22|Numbers 23:22}}; {{Numbers 24:8|24:8}}; {{Deuteronomy 33:17|Deuteronomy 33:17}}; {{Psalm 29:6|Psalms 29:6}}; {{Psalm 92:10|92:10}}; compare {{Genesis 1:28|Genesis 1:28}}; {{Genesis 9:2|9:2}}; {{Psalm 8:5-6|Psalm 8:5–6}}).
In the ancient Near East, people believed *the ostrich* was a bird that God had not given wisdom.

The ostrich symbolizes neglect for her young because she ({{Lamentations 4:3|Lamentations 4:3}}): 

- *Leaves her eggs on the ground*.

- Seems to abandon her eggs when a predator comes near. She is probably trying to distract the predator from the nest.

- Lays her eggs with other female ostrich in a shared nest, so many eggs are *not her own.*
*laughs at the horse and its rider*: See {{Job 39:7|39:7}}, {{Job 39:22|22}}; {{Job 41:29|41:29}}.
They blew *the ram's horn* in battle to signal the attack ({{Joshua 6:4-6|Joshua 6:4–6}}).
Where there is a dead body, you will find the eagle feeding on the remains ({{Ezekiel 39:17-19|Ezekiel 39:17–19}}; {{Matthew 24:28|Matthew 24:28}}; {{Luke 17:37|Luke 17:37}}).
The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) does not include the end of God's first speech.

Job's short and humble reply does not admit guilt, but it does admit how "insignificant" he is ({{Job 40:4|40:4}}). Earlier, he believed he could approach God like a prince or even question him ({{Job 31:37|31:37}}; {{Job 13:22-23|13:22–23}}).

- *I am insignificant* (compare {{Job 42:6|42:6}}): Job was not asking God to forgive his sin. Like Abraham, he recognized that he was not worthy ({{Genesis 18:27|Genesis 18:27}}).

- Job had asked those comforting him to cover their mouths to show shock ({{Job 21:5|21:5}}). Here, he does so himself in reaction to his own inappropriate words.
*I have nothing to add*: He had no more accusations against God and would not argue again.
*The LORD* repeated his earlier challenge (refer to {{Job 38:1-3|38:1–3}}).

In his second answer to God Job recognised something important. He hadn’t understood what he was talking about when he spoke with his friends. He had talked about things that were too wonderful for him to know. This means that they were things that human beings can’t understand.

Recognising this made Job humble. Job said that he hated himself. This doesn’t mean that Job thought he was a terrible person. It doesn’t mean that he had no love for himself. It means that he no longer wanted to argue against God. Job stopped bringing charges against God for treating him unfairly.

God had showed Job how much care he takes of all of his creatures. Job came to understand that he was one of God’s creatures. So Job understood that he could trust God because God was his creator. God had shown himself to Job. When Job heard and understood God, he saw that God was worthy of his trust.
Job's words had angered Elihu ({{Job 10:7|10:7}}; {{Job 27:2|27:2}}; {{Job 31:35-37|31:35–37}}; {{Job 32:2|32:2}}; {{Job 34:5|34:5}}). Now, God himself challenged Job's words.

Job could not humble proud people without God's authority ({{Isaiah 2:11-12|Isaiah 2:11–12}}, {{Isaiah 2:17|17}}; {{James 4:6|James 4:6}}; {{1 Peter 5:5-6|1 Peter 5:5–6}}; {{Malachi 4:3|Malachi 4:3}}; {{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}).

- After listing natural animals, God described *Behemoth* and "Leviathan" as creatures humans cannot control ({{Job 39:1-30|39:1–30}}; {{Job 40:15-24|40:15–24}}; {{Job 41:1-34|41:1–34}}). Job could not control the wild donkey or *ox* ({{Job 39:5-12|39:5–12}}; {{Job 40:15-24|40:15–24}}). However, God created and could control them, and Job had to accept this fact ({{Job 41:2|41:2}}).

- Here, *Behemoth* appears to be a natural creature: 

- It is an animal God made, just as he made Job ({{Job 40:15|40:15}}).

- It is not a fierce predator but eats *grass like an ox* ({{Job 40:15|40:15}}).

- It is in a poem about God’s creation of the natural world, not in a myth about the world's formation. Most commentators think *Behemoth* is the hippopotamus, a large, grass-eating animal ({{Job 40:15-19|40:15–19}}). It rests in the river among lotus plants and reeds ({{Job 40:21|40:21}}). Like the wild *ox, Behemoth* is strong ({{Job 40:16-18|40:16–18}}, {{Job 40:24|24}}; {{Job 39:11|39:11}}). Yet it is mostly peaceful ({{Job 40:20-23|40:20–23}}).

Unlike the peaceful Behemoth ({{Job 40:15-24|Job 40:15–24}}), Leviathan was a threat (see also {{Job 3:8|Job 3:8}}; {{Psalm 74:14|Psalms 74:14}}; {{Psalm 104:26|104:26}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}). Most scholars think Leviathan was like a crocodile, with its powerful jaws and tough skin twisting and turning in the water ({{Job 41:14|Job 41:14}}; {{Job 41:15-17|41:15–17}}, {{Job 41:23|23}}; {{Job 41:31-32|41:31–32}}). But Leviathan is a fire-breathing dragon that wraps around the sun to cause the sun to seem covered ({{Job 41:18-21|41:18–21}}; {{Job 3:8-9|3:8–9}}). 

The background for Leviathan is the seven-headed sea monster symbolizing chaos in ancient Near Eastern mythology. In the Bible, this wild sea creature often represents chaos and evil, whose head the Lord crushes ({{Psalm 74:14|Psalm 74:14}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}; compare {{Job 9:13|Job 9:13}}; {{Job 26:12|26:12}}; {{Psalm 89:9-10|Psalm 89:9–10}}; {{Isaiah 30:7|Isaiah 30:7}}; {{Isaiah 51:9|51:9}}). Later in the Bible, Satan is linked to the ancient serpent and great dragon ({{Genesis 3:1-24|Genesis 3}}; {{Revelation 12:9|Revelation 12:9}}; {{Revelation 20:2|20:2}}). Christ and his followers crush his head ({{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}).

Job understood the message of God’s speeches: *I know that You can do all things*. Nothing is too hard for him ({{Genesis 18:14|Genesis 18:14}}; {{Jeremiah 32:17|Jeremiah 32:17}}; {{Matthew 19:26|Matthew 19:26}}). Job says, *No plan of Yours can be thwarted* ({{Job 23:13|Job 23:13}}; {{Isaiah 14:27|Isaiah 14:27}}; {{Isaiah 46:10|46:10}}). Job realized how different he was from God.

*now my eyes have seen You*: Before this, Job had not *seen* God (see {{Job 23:8|23:8}}). Now, like the prophet Isaiah, he has been in God's presence and feels overwhelmed by how holy God is ({{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}).

- *Eliphaz the Temanite* was the spokesperson for the friends, probably because of he was older. Eliphaz had a false claim that his advice came from visions of prophecy ({{Job 4:12-16|4:12–16}}). Now God spoke to him, but not to support his message.

- Unlike his three friends, Job spoke accurately about God (compare {{Job 13:7-10|13:7–10}}). Job’s direct questions were more effective in finding out the truth about God than the friends’ shallow definitions of doctrine.

Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar had said things that weren’t true about God. They had said foolish things about God’s reasons for allowing Job to be tested. God was angry about this.

After they made a sacrifice and Job prayed for them, God forgave them. God called Job his servant. This meant that Job did the work that God gave him to do. God said that Job had spoken what was true about God.

This includes the questions Job asked. It includes Job talking about being sad, angry and confused. It includes Job longing to see God and to speak with him face to face. What God said about Job showed that Job passed the test that Satan had suggested. Job had continued to respect God. He respected God even when it seemed that God wasn’t blessing anything in his life.

When the test was over things once again went very well with Job. In this way something that Job’s friends had said came true in Job’s life. Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar and Elihu had recognised a pattern in life. That pattern was about people who obey and serve God. Elihu had said that things will go well with those who do this.

God blessed Job with success again and gave him more than he had before the test. He gave Job more of everything that people in his time could hope for. This included many children, livestock, honour and long life.

- *The LORD *made *Job* the "mediator" that *Job* had hoped to find for himself and that Elihu wanted to be ({{Job 9:33|9:33}}; {{Job 16:19-21|16:19–21}}; {{Job 19:25|19:25}}; {{Job 32:1-37:24|32:1–37:24}}).

- *go to My servant Job*: God wanted Job’s friends to make peace with *Job* before they offered their gifts ({{Matthew 5:23-24|Matthew 5:23–24}}).

- *My servant Job will pray for you*: He had also prayed for his children ({{Job 1:5|1:5}}; compare {{James 5:16|James 5:16}}; {{1 John 5:16|1 John 5:16}}).

- When *the LORD *accepted Job’s prayer, it ironically fulfilled Eliphaz’s promise ({{Job 22:26-30|Job 22:26–30}}).
Job's fortunes probably included his health ({{Job 42:16-17|42:16–17}}). God created humans to bless them, not to do them harm (curse).

- Even though God restored Job, he still needed comfort for the loss of his children. His family and former friends continued to support him, following Job's earlier practices, taking over where the three friends had stopped ({{Job 4:4|4:4}}; {{Job 16:5|16:5}}; {{Job 2:11|2:11}}; compare {{2 Corinthians 7:6|2 Corinthians 7:6}}).

- The money given to Job was not just charity to increase his wealth again. It was also to honor him and gain favor from an influential man (for example, {{Proverbs 18:16|Proverbs 18:16}}). It might also have been to ease any lack of favor (for example, {{Genesis 32:20|Genesis 32:20}}; {{Genesis 33:10|33:10}}; {{Genesis 43:11|43:11}}; {{1 Samuel 25:27|1 Samuel 25:27}}).

- Women wore* a gold ring* in their nose ({{Genesis 24:47|Genesis 24:47}}; {{Proverbs 11:22|Proverbs 11:22}}; {{Isaiah 3:21|Isaiah 3:21}}). Both men and women wore them on the ears ({{Genesis 35:4|Genesis 35:4}}; {{Exodus 32:2-3|Exodus 32:2–3}}; {{Judges 8:24|Judges 8:24}}).
When God blessed Job, it ironically fulfilled Bildad’s promise ({{Job 8:7|8:7}}).

- The names of Job’s new daughters reflect his good fortune God had renewed: 

- *Jemimah* means “dove” (see {{Song of Songs 2:14|Song 2:14}}). 

- *Keziah* means “cassia” or “cinnamon flower” (see {{Psalm 45:8|Psalm 45:8}}). 

- *Keren-happuch* means “horn of antimony,” which is a shiny container for make-up.

*their father granted them an inheritance among their brothers: *Daughters usually inherited only if there were no male children ({{Numbers 27:1-23|Numbers 27}}; {{Numbers 36:1-13|36}}). Perhaps Job's unusual action indicated his great wealth. Only a rich man could give some wealth to the families into which his daughters would marry.

- Job lived for 140 more years, which was about twice as long as a normal life ({{Psalm 90:10|Psalm 90:10}}). If God gave him double what he had before ({{Job 42:10|Job 42:10}}), Job may have already been 70 years old, making his total life 210 years. This would fit the time of the early patriarchs in the Bible (see {{Genesis 25:7|Genesis 25:7}}; {{Genesis 35:28|35:28}}; {{Genesis 47:28|47:28}}; {{Genesis 50:26|50:26}}; {{Deuteronomy 34:7|Deuteronomy 34:7}}; {{Joshua 24:29|Joshua 24:29}}). 

- *to the fourth generation*: God blessed Job by letting him live long enough to see his children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and great-great-grandchildren grow up ({{Genesis 50:23|Genesis 50:23}}; {{Psalm 128:6|Psalm 128:6}}).

- The patriarchs ("first fathers") Abraham and Isaac also died at an old age ({{Genesis 25:8|Genesis 25:8}}; {{Genesis 35:29|35:29}}). Job too lived a long, full life. This fulfilled Eliphaz’s promise ({{Job 5:26|Job 5:26}}). His promise had its basis on God's general promise ({{Deuteronomy 6:2|Deuteronomy 6:2}}; {{Psalm 91:16|Psalm 91:16}}).

- At the end of the book, the ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) adds a note saying that Job will resurrect from the dead at the final resurrection. It also provides information about where and when Job and those who descended from him lived.
